items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Casper, WY
items.meta: Casper, WY built its identity on the Salt Creek oil field a century ago. Get a courthouse-grounded, honest read on your Natrona County mineral interest.

sections.html:
Casper earned the nickname Oil City for a reason. Salt Creek, discovered north of town in the early 1900s, was one of the largest oil fields in the country at the time, and it built the refineries that shaped this city for a century.

That history means Natrona County has a longer, deeper record of mineral ownership, leasing, and litigation than almost anywhere else in Wyoming. We have pulled deeds here that trace back through five or six owners over a hundred years, some tied to still-producing units, others to acreage that's sat quiet since the last boom.

If you're holding a Casper-area mineral interest, whether it's a family legacy piece or something you bought more recently, we want your actual documentation, deed, royalty statements, probate order, before we quote a single number, because this county has too much variation for guesswork.

sections.title: Salt Creek's long production history
sections.html:
Salt Creek has produced for more than a century, moving through primary recovery, waterflood, and further enhanced-recovery phases as operators kept finding ways to extend the field's life. That longevity gives mineral owners inside the unit real documented royalty history to price against, something a lot of newer Wyoming plays simply don't have.

Decline on a field this mature tends to be gentle year over year rather than the steep early drop-off you'd see from a new horizontal well, which changes how we think about remaining value.

sections.title: A century of refining and industry around the field
sections.html: Casper's refineries and midstream infrastructure grew up around Salt Creek's output, and that industrial history shows up in local land records in ways that matter for title work, old right-of-way grants, easements, and multiple rounds of corporate mergers among the operators who've held leases here over the decades. Untangling which current entity actually holds an old lease is sometimes its own small research project.

sections.title: Pricing a Casper-area interest
sections.html: For producing interests, we lead with your trailing royalty statements and the unit's current enhanced-recovery status. For undeveloped acreage elsewhere in the county, we price against recent comparable Natrona County trades. Either way, we confirm your title through the county recorder before quoting anything.

sections.title: Build the County-Record Packet
sections.html: A town name is only the first line of a Wyoming mineral file. The working packet should connect the tract to the county, legal description, section, township, range, owner name, vesting instrument, reservations, lease, division order, payor record, and any probate or trust document that changed the chain. Local field history belongs beside the recorded evidence, not in place of it. Where fee minerals meet federal or state ownership, the packet should also identify which tract, depth, or formation is actually private and conveyable before any acreage or paid decimal is carried into an offer.

sections.title: Keep the Paid Interest and the Deed Scope Aligned
sections.html: A royalty statement can show what is being paid on a tract, but the statement does not by itself prove the full mineral estate. The review should reconcile the paid decimal to the ownership fraction, lease royalty, unit allocation, well, product, production month, deductions, taxes, suspense, and any adjustment line. The proposed deed and written purchase scope should then repeat the verified owner, county, legal description, included depths or formations, effective date, conveyed fraction, retained interest, pre-closing proceeds, title conditions, and recording instructions. Any mismatch stays on the curative list until the supporting record resolves it.

faqs.q: Is Salt Creek still producing after all this time?
faqs.a: Yes, portions continue under enhanced recovery. We will check the current status specific to your interest.

faqs.q: Your lease has changed hands between operators multiple times. Does that matter?
faqs.a: It affects who currently administers your royalty payments, but not your underlying ownership. We will trace the current operator of record.

faqs.q: What if your interest is undeveloped, away from Salt Creek?
faqs.a: We will price it as speculative acreage based on comparable Natrona County trades, distinct from producing minerals.

faqs.q: How fast can a Casper-area sale close?
faqs.a: Once title is confirmed, typically a few weeks, sometimes faster with clean, well-documented ownership.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Gillette, WY
items.meta: Gillette sits in Powder River Basin coal and horizontal oil activity. Get a fair cash offer for your Campbell County mineral interest.

sections.html:
Gillette calls itself the Energy Capital of the Nation for a reason. Coal, coalbed methane, and now horizontal oil have all run through Campbell County ground within a single working lifetime.

That layered history means mineral owners around Gillette often hold interests touched by more than one boom. A family that leased for CBM in the early 2000s, watched that play crash, and now finds a horizontal Niobrara or Turner well going in on the same section isn't an unusual story here.

sections.title: From coalbed methane bust to horizontal oil
sections.html: The CBM boom peaked in the mid-2000s and collapsed hard when gas prices fell and shallow coal wells stopped penciling. Plenty of Campbell County mineral owners wrote that era off as a wash. Then operators came back with horizontal wells targeting the Niobrara, Turner, Sussex, and Parkman formations thousands of feet deeper, and some of that same ground got leased and drilled again.

sections.title: Coal royalties are their own animal
sections.html: Gillette sits atop some of the largest coal reserves in the country, and coal royalty payments run on a different mechanism than oil and gas, tied to surface or federal coal leases and production reports rather than a wellhead meter. If your interest includes coal, keep that royalty stream separate in your mind from any oil and gas minerals on the same land.

sections.title: Why fractional ownership runs deep here
sections.html: Decades of drilling, unitization, and family transfers mean a lot of Campbell County minerals sit in small decimal interests spread across siblings, cousins, and trusts. Untangling exactly what you own before selling is often the biggest time cost, more than negotiating the price itself.

Rock Springs has a longer industrial history than almost anywhere else in Wyoming — coal first, then natural gas from the uplift's Fort Union and Mesaverde sands, and trona mining that has run continuously for decades to supply soda ash production worldwide. For a mineral owner, the practical question is which of these your deed actually covers, because oil and gas rights and solid mineral rights like trona are sometimes held by entirely different parties even under the same tract.

As the largest city in Sweetwater County, Rock Springs is also where most of the county's mineral title paperwork ultimately gets recorded, which helps our review move quickly once we have your legal description.

items.meta: Buffalo, WY is the Johnson County seat on the Powder River Basin's western edge, coalbed methane history and conventional oil both in play here.

sections.html:
Buffalo is the Johnson County seat, sitting where the Bighorn Mountains meet the western edge of the Powder River Basin, and the mineral history under this county runs through both a coalbed methane boom and a much older conventional oil story.

Johnson County saw real coalbed methane development during the boom years of the late 1990s and 2000s, when operators targeted shallow coal seams for methane gas across the Powder River Basin, before that play largely went bust as gas prices collapsed and a lot of those wells were plugged or abandoned. Older, deeper conventional production has a longer history in pockets of the county as well.

If your family's interest around Buffalo traces to that CBM era, we want to know whether the wells are still producing, plugged, or somewhere in between, because that status changes everything about what the interest is worth today.

Coalbed methane wells produce differently than conventional oil and gas, they often start slow while water is pumped off the coal seam, then ramp up gas production before declining. When prices crashed, a lot of Powder River Basin CBM wells stopped being economic to operate, and many were plugged well before their reserves were fully depleted.

That history means some Johnson County royalty owners saw checks that started, grew, then simply stopped years ago. If that's your situation, your interest still has value, priced on whether the underlying wellbore could realistically be reactivated or re-drilled, not on the current absence of a check.

sections.title: Older conventional production
sections.html: Beneath and alongside the CBM-era wells, Johnson County has pockets of older, deeper conventional oil production that predates the coalbed boom entirely. These tend to be lower-volume, longer-lived assets with their own separate lease and royalty history, distinct from the CBM story even on the same or adjacent tracts.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Big Horn County, WY
items.meta: Own mineral rights in Big Horn County, WY? This is legacy Bighorn Basin oil ground, Elk Basin and Byron fields, split estate, decades of family fractions.

sections.html:
Big Horn County sits on some of the oldest producing oil ground in Wyoming, and the courthouse in Basin holds nearly a century of leases, deeds, and probate filings to prove it.

The Bighorn Basin's early oil fields came in fast in the 1910s and 20s, when Elk Basin, Byron, Grass Creek, and Garland turned this stretch of north-central Wyoming into a working oilfield years before most of the rest of the state saw a rig. That early start means Big Horn County carries a longer, more tangled ownership history than newer plays, deeds that reference original homestead patents, probate orders spanning three or four generations, and mineral fractions split so many times that a single quarter section might list a dozen owners.

We have spent enough time in the county recorder's office in Basin to know how to read that history. Most of the calls we get from Big Horn County owners start the same way: someone found an old deed, or a royalty check finally stopped coming, and nobody in the family knows what it means anymore. We can usually tell you within a few days.

sections.title: The legacy fields that built this county
sections.html:
Elk Basin straddles the Wyoming-Montana line near Deaver and Frannie, and it's been producing since 1915, one of the true old-guard Wyoming oil fields. Byron field, right around the town that shares its name, has similarly deep roots. Both fields have gone through primary production, then secondary waterflood recovery, and in some cases tertiary methods to keep pulling oil from formations that have been worked for over a hundred years.

That longevity is a double-edged sword for mineral owners. On one hand, it means there's real, documented royalty history to price an interest against if your tract sits inside a producing unit. On the other, decline curves on fields this mature are typically gentle but modest, nothing like the steep early production numbers you'd see out of a new horizontal well elsewhere in the state.

Grass Creek and Oregon Basin, technically straddling into neighboring Park County, round out the historic core that put this part of the Bighorn Basin on the map before most other Wyoming plays existed.

sections.title: Split estate and old homestead patents
sections.html:
Much of Big Horn County was settled under the Homestead Act and later reclamation-era irrigation projects, particularly around the Shoshone and Bighorn River bottomland near Basin, Burlington, Cowley, and Deaver. Many of those original patents included full mineral rights, which families later severed off through lease bonuses or outright sales during exploration booms.

The result today is a lot of split estate: one owner on the surface, farming or ranching the ground, and a different set of owners, often scattered heirs, holding the mineral interest beneath it. Confirming which situation applies to your specific tract is the first thing we do, because it changes both what you own and how a sale would work.

sections.title: Untangling multi-generation fractions
sections.html:
Because so many Big Horn County mineral interests trace back to homesteads from the 1900s and 1910s, it's common for a single interest to have passed through three, four, or even five rounds of inheritance by now. We have worked files where an eighth-generation fraction of a quarter section is split between a dozen cousins who've never met each other.

That doesn't make the interest impossible to sell, it just means the title work takes patience. We pull the recorder's grantor-grantee index in Basin, trace the probate orders where they exist, and confirm exactly what percentage of what acreage you hold before we ever quote a number. If co-owners want to sell together, we can coordinate that too, but we will always price your specific fraction on its own merits first.

sections.title: What actually drives value here
sections.html:
For a producing interest inside an active Elk Basin, Byron, or Grass Creek unit, we look at your trailing royalty statements and the field's current secondary or tertiary recovery status to gauge remaining runway. For undeveloped acreage away from those trends, we price against recent comparable Big Horn County transactions, adjusted for proximity to production.

Either way, we never quote a flat per-acre number without checking your specific tract first. Big Horn County has too much variation, mature waterflood units next to acreage that's never seen a permit, for a one-size number to mean anything honest.

faqs.a: Byron, Deaver, Cowley, and Burlington all sit near or within legacy field boundaries, with Basin serving as the county seat where the records are filed. We will check your specific location against current unit maps.

faqs.q: Your family's mineral interest has passed through several estates. Where do you start?

faqs.a: Portions remain active under secondary recovery. We will check the current status tied to your specific interest before discussing value.

faqs.q: How is a mature field priced compared to a new play elsewhere in Wyoming?
faqs.a: Mature fields typically show gentler decline but less speculative upside. We price against actual trailing royalty history rather than assumptions borrowed from newer, unrelated plays.

faqs.a: No. Split estate is common throughout Big Horn County, and mineral sales are entirely separate from surface ownership, grazing, or farming operations.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Campbell County, WY
items.meta: Own mineral rights in Campbell County, WY? Gillette-area CBM boom-and-bust, coal split estate, and horizontal Niobrara/Turner activity, get a real read here.

sections.html:
Campbell County has three distinct mineral stories layered on top of each other around Gillette, coal, coalbed methane, and now horizontal oil, and knowing which one your interest belongs to changes everything about how we would price it.

This is the country's largest coal-producing county, home to massive surface mines like Black Thunder and North Antelope Rochelle that supply a meaningful share of the nation's thermal coal. But Campbell County's oil and gas history runs just as deep: it was ground zero for the Powder River Basin's coalbed methane boom in the late 1990s and 2000s, when thousands of shallow wells were drilled to produce methane trapped in the basin's coal seams, before low gas prices collapsed that economics and left a lot of it plugged or idle.

More recently, operators including EOG Resources and others have targeted deeper, stacked conventional and unconventional zones, the Niobrara, Turner, Sussex, Parkman, and Frontier formations, with horizontal wells and dense multi-well pad development around Gillette and Wright. If you're holding a Campbell County mineral interest, we need to know which of these three stories, coal, CBM, or the newer stacked-lateral oil plays, actually applies to your specific tract before we can give you an honest number.

sections.title: Coal and split estate
sections.html:
Campbell County's surface coal mines operate under a split-estate arrangement that's different from oil and gas leasing: much of the coal itself is federally owned and leased through the Bureau of Land Management, while private surface owners negotiate separate surface-use agreements with the mining companies. If your family's mineral interest includes coal rights specifically, that's typically a separate legal question from oil and gas rights on the same or adjacent land, and we will help you understand which you actually hold.

Most of what we buy and sell day to day is oil and gas mineral interest, not coal, but we always check what's actually described in your deed before assuming.

sections.title: The coalbed methane boom and bust
sections.html:
CBM wells here produced water first, then ramping gas, from thousands of shallow completions across the basin through the 2000s. When gas prices fell, a large share of those wells stopped being economic, and many were plugged well before their coal seam reserves were exhausted. If your royalty checks from a CBM well slowed to nothing years ago, that's an extremely common story in this county, not a sign your interest lacks value entirely.

We check the specific well's plugged or idle status through state records before pricing a dormant CBM interest, since a plugged well and a temporarily idle one are priced very differently.

sections.title: Stacked-lateral horizontal development
sections.html:
Beneath the CBM-era wellbores, operators have spent the last decade-plus drilling horizontal laterals through multiple stacked formations, the Niobrara, Turner, Sussex, Parkman, and Frontier, sometimes from the same well pad targeting different zones. This is genuinely active, ongoing development in parts of the county, particularly around Gillette and south toward Wright, and interests inside these units can carry real current royalty income.

Spacing and unitization on these stacked plays tend to be denser than older conventional development, which affects how your net mineral acreage translates into your actual royalty share.

sections.title: Confirming which story is yours
sections.html: We pull the Campbell County recorder's lease and deed history for your specific section, cross-reference well status through the Wyoming Oil and Gas Conservation Commission, and identify whether your interest sits in a coal-only area, a dormant CBM unit, an active stacked-lateral development, or genuinely undeveloped acreage. Only then do we quote a number, and we will explain exactly which category yours falls into and why.

sections.title: Why Gillette records take longer to sort out
sections.html:
Because this county has seen three distinct waves of mineral development layered on top of each other, coal leasing in the mid-twentieth century, CBM in the 2000s, and stacked-lateral horizontal drilling more recently, the paper trail on a given tract can run long. We have traced Campbell County interests through lease assignments that changed hands four or five times as operators consolidated, sold off, or exited the basin entirely during the CBM downturn.

That complexity is exactly why we do not quote a Campbell County interest sight unseen. Every layer of history matters to getting the number right, and skipping the research just shifts the risk onto you.

faqs.a: Yes, though it's priced differently than active production. We will check the well's plugged status and any redevelopment potential before quoting.

faqs.q: Do you own coal rights or oil and gas rights, or both?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on your deed language. We will review what you have and tell you clearly which mineral rights you actually hold.

faqs.q: Is there active drilling in Campbell County right now?
faqs.a: Yes, horizontal development in the Niobrara, Turner, and other stacked zones continues in parts of the county, particularly toward Wright. We will check your specific section.

faqs.q: How do surface coal mines affect your mineral interest?
faqs.a: Only if your interest overlaps an active or permitted coal mine boundary, and even then the effect depends on your specific deed and surface-use agreements. We will clarify your situation.

faqs.q: What's the difference in how you'd price a coal interest versus an oil and gas interest?
faqs.a: Coal is typically leased through federal or long-term royalty structures tied to production volume, while oil and gas prices against decline curves and current commodity markets. We only buy oil and gas minerals, and we will tell you plainly if your interest is coal instead.

items.meta: Own mineral rights in Converse County, WY? Douglas and Glenrock sit inside one of Wyoming's most active stacked-lateral horizontal oil plays. Get a real read.

sections.html:
Converse County has been ground zero for one of Wyoming's most active horizontal drilling booms of the past decade, and if you're holding a mineral interest around Douglas or Glenrock, there's a real chance it's tied to genuinely current production.

Operators including Devon Energy, Chesapeake, Continental Resources, and others have drilled dense multi-well pads targeting stacked pay zones here, the Niobrara, Turner, and Sussex formations chief among them, often from a single surface location with laterals reaching out in multiple directions to drain different intervals at different depths. This kind of stacked-lateral development has made Converse County one of the more actively drilled counties in the state through much of the 2010s and into the 2020s.

That density changes what we need from you before pricing an interest. Because so many wells here were drilled recently, with modern completion techniques, decline curves and unit configurations vary a lot even within a few miles, and we lean heavily on your actual trailing royalty statements rather than county-wide assumptions.

sections.title: Stacked pay and horizontal density
sections.html:
Where an older Wyoming field might have one productive zone, Converse County's newer development often targets three or four stacked intervals from the same well pad. That means a single spacing unit can have multiple horizontal wellbores contributing to your royalty check, which is part of why interests here can carry meaningfully more current income than comparable acreage in a single-zone field elsewhere in the state.

It also means unitization and pooling paperwork around here tends to be more complex than older, simpler conventional leases. We take the time to read through it rather than skip to a number.

Douglas, the county seat, and Glenrock to the west have both served as staging points for drilling activity that's radiated out across the county over the past decade. Courthouse records in Douglas reflect that pace, with lease filings, unit agreements, and division orders processed at a volume this county hadn't seen since much older conventional development decades earlier.

If your family's interest sits inside one of these newer horizontal units, your production history is probably recent enough that we can price it with real precision rather than broad estimates.

sections.title: Commodity exposure and decline behavior

Where your specific wells sit on that curve, combined with current oil price levels, drives most of what your interest is worth today. We never quote a flat number without seeing your actual statements first, because this play moves too much with the market for that to be honest.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Daniel, WY
items.meta: Daniel, WY sits between the Pinedale gas fields and the Green River headwaters in Sublette County. Get an honest read on your mineral interest before selling.

sections.html:
Daniel sits close enough to Pinedale that we always check whether a tract here falls inside the Anticline's productive unit boundary before assuming it's just quiet ranch ground.

This is historic cattle country, site of one of the earliest cattle drives in Wyoming history, but it also sits near enough to the Pinedale Anticline's tight-gas development that some Daniel-area sections do carry real lease and production history. Others, further from the field's core, remain undeveloped acreage that's never drawn operator interest.

We check your exact legal description against the current unit boundary before telling you anything, since the difference between inside and outside the field changes the entire pricing conversation.

sections.title: Ranch history over a productive gas field
sections.html:
The Green River drainage through this part of Sublette County has been cattle country since before the oil industry existed here, and a lot of Daniel-area mineral interests trace to those original ranch homesteads. What's changed is that some of that ground now sits over, or adjacent to, active Pinedale Anticline tight-gas development.

Determining which situation applies to your family's specific tract is the first and most important step before we discuss any number.

sections.title: Pricing depends on your exact position
sections.html:
For tracts with real production, we work from your trailing royalty statements and where the underlying wells sit on their decline curve. For undeveloped acreage nearby, we price against comparable recent Sublette County trades. Both are legitimate assets, just priced on entirely different bases.

The Green River Drift, the annual cattle drive route that runs near here, is a reminder of just how long this ground has been worked as ranch land, long before anyone thought about what was underneath it. That history is part of why so many mineral interests here trace to a single original family.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Deaver, WY
items.meta: Deaver, WY sits at the Montana line near the historic Elk Basin field. Get a courthouse-checked, honest read on your Big Horn County mineral interest.

sections.html:
Deaver sits right at the state line, close to Frannie, and Elk Basin field straddles the border directly through this corner of Big Horn County.

This field has produced continuously since 1915, one of the true legacy assets of the Bighorn Basin, and its long life has meant repeated rounds of secondary and enhanced recovery to keep pulling oil from formations tapped over a hundred years ago. Big Horn County recorder records around Deaver go back accordingly far, with leases, unit agreements, and probate transfers reflecting several generations of ownership.

If your family's interest sits inside or near the Elk Basin boundary, there's real production history worth checking. We will confirm your specific position before saying anything about value.

sections.title: A border field with a long memory

Because Elk Basin crosses into Montana, unit administration and royalty payments here sometimes involve coordination across both states. We make sure your Wyoming-side ownership is confirmed cleanly through Big Horn County records regardless of how the broader unit is structured.

The field's continued investment in enhanced recovery after this many decades signals there's still oil worth chasing here, which affects how we think about remaining value in a producing interest.

Frannie and Deaver share this border stretch, and we have traced ownership across both towns for families whose land holdings spanned the two communities. Confirming which specific section your interest falls in matters more than which town address is on the deed.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Diamondville, WY
items.meta: Diamondville, WY sits next to Kemmerer's coal and trona country in Lincoln County. Get a straight read on your mineral interest, oil, gas, or otherwise.

sections.html:
Diamondville sits practically on top of Kemmerer, and this corner of Lincoln County built its history on coal mining first, oil and gas leasing second, which means we always check exactly what kind of minerals your deed actually describes.

The coal seams that fed Kemmerer's mines for a century sit under a lot of this ground, and separately, Overthrust Belt oil and gas leasing has swept through the broader area in cycles since the 1970s. A single family's mineral history here can include both, an old coal lease from one generation and an oil and gas lease from another, on the same or adjacent land.

Before we quote you anything, we need to know which minerals your deed actually covers, because coal and oil and gas are priced through completely different mechanisms.

sections.title: Coal country roots
sections.html: Kemmerer's coal mining history predates most of the oil and gas leasing activity in this part of the state, and a lot of original land patents in the area reserved or conveyed coal rights separately from other minerals. If your deed specifically addresses coal, that's a different kind of asset than oil and gas, typically administered through longer-term royalty arrangements tied to mining volume.

sections.title: Oil and gas leasing history
sections.html:
Separately, this area saw Overthrust Belt leasing pushes over the decades, mostly without production this close to Diamondville itself, since the belt's productive fields sit further east. Oil and gas interests here typically price as undeveloped, speculative acreage rather than anything currently producing.

We check the Lincoln County recorder's specific lease and deed history for your tract before saying which situation, coal, oil and gas, or both, applies to you.

Diamondville and Kemmerer have essentially grown together over the decades, and old deeds sometimes use one town name or the other interchangeably for the same legal description. That's not usually a problem for confirming ownership, but it's worth knowing before you assume a deed refers to a different tract than it actually does.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in East Thermopolis, WY
items.meta: East Thermopolis sits near Hamilton Dome, one of Wyoming's oldest oil fields, producing since 1918. Get an honest read on your Hot Springs County interest.

sections.html:
Hamilton Dome field, just outside East Thermopolis, has been producing oil since 1918, making it one of the oldest continuously developed fields anywhere in Wyoming.

This is a field with more than a century of leasing, drilling, and enhanced-recovery investment behind it, and Hot Springs County recorder records reflect that entire span, deeds and probate transfers stacked across five or six generations of ownership in some cases. The town itself is known for its hot springs and mineral baths, but the mineral interests we work with here are the oil and gas kind, tied to a field that's genuinely outlasted most of its Wyoming contemporaries.

If your family's interest connects to Hamilton Dome, we check current production and enhanced-recovery status before saying anything about value, since a field this mature is priced very differently than newer Wyoming plays.

sections.title: Over a century of production
sections.html:
Hamilton Dome has moved through primary recovery, waterflood, and further enhanced-recovery phases over its long life, the kind of sustained reinvestment that signals real remaining reserves rather than a played-out field. That history gives mineral owners inside the unit boundary genuine, long-documented royalty history to price an interest against.

Decline on an asset this mature tends to be gradual, a different shape entirely than the steep early drop-off from a new horizontal well in a place like Converse County.

sections.title: Untangling a century of inheritance
sections.html:
With ownership this old, it's common for a Hamilton Dome-area interest to have passed through numerous estates since the original lease was signed in the early twentieth century. We trace the Hot Springs County recorder's grantor-grantee index as far back as necessary to confirm your exact fractional share, working from whatever documentation you have, even a partial or very old deed.

Hot Springs County is the smallest county in Wyoming by population, and its recorder's office reflects that scale, records that are thorough but not always digitized. We are used to working through paper files here when necessary to confirm a chain of title properly.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Eden, WY
items.meta: Eden, WY sits in an irrigated valley near Sweetwater County's Continental Divide gas trend and the Union Pacific checkerboard. Get an honest mineral read.

sections.html:
Eden sits in an irrigated farming valley that got its name from the reclamation project that turned this stretch of high desert green, and it also sits close enough to the checkerboard and the Continental Divide gas trend that we check both before saying anything about a mineral interest here.

The Eden Valley Irrigation Project brought farming to this part of Sweetwater County in the early twentieth century, and the original patents came with mineral rights attached, some later severed off through leasing during oil and gas exploration pushes. Separately, this whole corridor along the old Union Pacific right-of-way carries the checkerboard pattern of alternating private and federal sections.

Between farm-family mineral history and the checkerboard's private-versus-federal question, there are two things we need to sort out before quoting you anything, and we will walk through both.

sections.title: Irrigated farmland with severed minerals
sections.html: A lot of Eden-area mineral interests trace to the original reclamation-era homestead patents, split off from the farm surface through decades of leasing and inheritance. That mineral estate is entirely separate from irrigation water rights or the farming operation itself, whether or not the family still works the land.

sections.title: Checkerboard ownership nearby
sections.html: Depending on your exact section, your family's interest may trace to a private Union Pacific land grant patent, sellable outright, or to federally retained ground where any minerals are BLM-administered rather than privately held. We check each tract section by section rather than assuming based on the area generally.

sections.title: Nearby gas development
sections.html:
The Continental Divide-Creston gas trend runs through parts of Sweetwater County south and east of Eden, and some tracts in this broader area do carry production history. We check your specific legal description against current unit boundaries before saying whether that applies to you.

Between the irrigation history, the checkerboard, and the nearby gas trend, Eden-area ownership questions take a bit more digging than a simpler tract elsewhere in the state. We would rather take that extra time upfront than give you a number that doesn't hold up once someone looks closer.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Edgerton, WY
items.meta: Own minerals near Edgerton, WY on the old Salt Creek field? Get a fair cash offer for your Natrona County royalty or mineral interest, no obligation.

sections.html:
Edgerton sits on the edge of the Salt Creek field, one of the oldest producing oil fields in the Rocky Mountains. That history shows up in the deed room.

Salt Creek has been producing since before Wyoming had paved highways. Wells drilled in the 1910s and 1920s got re-drilled, unitized, and re-worked through half a dozen operator changes, and every one of those transactions left paper in the Natrona County Clerk's office. If you hold minerals under or near Edgerton, chances are your interest came down through a family that homesteaded here two or three generations ago and never sold, just kept cashing whatever check showed up.

sections.title: What's actually producing around Edgerton
sections.html: The shallow Salt Creek sands (Wall Creek, Second Wall Creek, Frontier) are mostly stripper production now, low volume, long decline curves, operated by smaller independents who bought the legacy leases off the majors decades back. Newer horizontal work in the deeper Niobrara and Turner has moved through parts of Natrona County too, and where those units overlap old Salt Creek acreage you can end up with two different operators sending two different statements for the same section.

sections.title: Why the ownership is usually split six ways
sections.html: Original Salt Creek-era mineral grants got willed, divorced, and probated across a century. A quarter section that started with one owner in 1918 might be held by fourteen heirs today, each with a sliver of a decimal interest. Small interests like that get expensive for operators to track and easy for owners to lose interest in, which is exactly when people start asking what the acreage is worth.

sections.title: Reading your Edgerton royalty check
sections.html: Stripper wells decline slow but steady, a few percent a year, so your check five years from now will likely be smaller than it is today even with no drop in price. Buyers price that decline into an offer. Bring your most recent two or three check stubs and your division order when you want a real number instead of a guess.

faqs.a: Most legacy Salt Creek-area interests are still on some kind of stripper production, even at low volume. Pull your last check stub or call the county clerk to confirm the well status before you assume it's dry.

faqs.q: What county records do you need?
faqs.a: Natrona County Clerk's office in Casper holds the deed and probate records. If your interest passed through an estate, bring the probate case number along with your deed.

faqs.q: Does age of the field lower the value?
faqs.a: It affects it, it doesn't kill it. Older stripper production is valued on current volume and decline, not on when the field was discovered. Newer horizontal activity nearby can also lift interest even on old legacy tracts.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Esterbrook, WY
items.meta: Hold mineral rights tied to Esterbrook or the Laramie Peak country in Converse County? Get a straightforward cash offer, no pressure, no games.

sections.html:
Esterbrook is mountain country, timber and ranchland below Laramie Peak, not the flat oil patch most people picture when they hear Converse County.

That doesn't mean the mineral estate under Esterbrook-area ranches is worthless. It means it behaves differently than the Niobrara and Turner units thirty miles north and east around Douglas and Glenrock. Most Esterbrook-area mineral owners hold acreage that's never been leased, or was leased once decades ago and let expire, because the drilling never reached that far up into the foothills.

sections.title: Why this ground stays quiet
sections.html: The productive Powder River Basin formations shallow out and thin toward the basin margin as you climb toward Laramie Peak. Operators chase the thick, pressured rock closer to the basin center. Esterbrook-area minerals sit on the flank, which means lower odds of a well ever getting drilled directly under your tract, though offset units nearby can still hold or drain adjacent sections.

sections.title: What sellers here are usually holding
sections.html: A lot of Converse County ranch families split the surface from the minerals generations back, sold the ranch, and kept the mineral rights as the one asset that couldn't be grazed off or fenced away. If that's your situation, you likely have a mineral deed with no current lease attached, which is a different kind of sale than an owner collecting active royalty checks.

sections.title: Selling unleased, undrilled minerals
sections.html: Unleased acreage sells for less per acre than producing minerals, obviously, but it still has value, especially if it sits inside a larger block that could interest an operator putting together a future unit. Bring your legal description and whatever old lease paperwork you can find, even expired leases, since they tell a buyer who's shown interest in the area before.

faqs.a: Check the Converse County Clerk's records in Douglas for any lease of record on your legal description, current or expired. Many flank tracts up here have one old lease from a boom year and nothing since.

faqs.q: Can you sell if there's no well and no lease?
faqs.a: Yes. Unleased minerals still trade, just at a lower multiple than producing acreage. The value comes from proximity to active drilling and the odds of future development.

faqs.q: Should you lease before you sell?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. A fresh lease can raise your sale price if a real operator signs it, but chasing a lease on flank ground with no drilling interest can just delay a sale that was going to happen anyway.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Etna, WY
items.meta: Own mineral rights under Etna in Star Valley, Lincoln County? See what's realistic for undeveloped or lightly-drilled acreage before you sell.

sections.html:
Etna is Star Valley, hay meadows and dairy country tucked against the Idaho line, not the gas fields on the other side of Lincoln County.

Ask a hundred people in Star Valley about their mineral rights and most will tell you nobody's ever drilled a well near them. That's mostly true. Star Valley sits west of the Overthrust Belt structures that made Kemmerer and the LaBarge area productive, and the geology under Etna hasn't drawn the same operator interest.

sections.title: Why Star Valley isn't the Overthrust Belt
sections.html: The thrust faulting that stacked up gas-bearing reservoirs east of here around the Moxa Arch and the Overthrust Belt proper doesn't carry the same way into the Star Valley trough. Etna-area minerals sit in a structural setting that hasn't produced the kind of trap operators drill for, which is the honest reason activity has stayed light.

sections.title: What that means for an Etna mineral owner
sections.html: If your family homesteaded or bought land here decades back and kept the minerals when the surface changed hands, you're likely holding an unleased, undrilled interest. Some owners assume that means zero value. It usually means modest value, priced against the small chance of future interest rather than a check you're already getting.

sections.title: What to have ready
sections.html: Your mineral deed and legal description are the starting point. If you've never leased, say so plainly, it's common here and doesn't need explaining or apologizing for. A buyer working this area knows Star Valley's history and will price accordingly.

sections.title: Estate settlements in Star Valley
sections.html: A lot of Etna-area mineral interests only surface when a probate attorney is settling a grandparent's estate and finds an old severance deed among the farm records. If that's how you found out you own minerals here, you're not alone, it's a common enough discovery in this valley that county clerk staff in Kemmerer see it regularly.

items.meta: Farson, WY landowner on the high desert checkerboard in Sweetwater County? Get a straightforward cash offer for your mineral interest.

sections.html:
Farson is high desert ranch country along the old Lander Trail, and the checkerboard survey pattern out here decides more about mineral ownership than most people realize.

This part of Sweetwater County was laid out under the 1862 Union Pacific railroad land grant, odd-numbered sections going to the railroad, even sections staying federal. A century and a half later, that pattern still shapes who owns the minerals under a Farson-area ranch and who's negotiating with the BLM next door on the section over.

If it traces back to a federal homestead patent, there's a real chance the minerals were reserved to the United States under the Stock-Raising Homestead Act, meaning you own the surface but the federal government, administered by the BLM, owns what's underneath.

sections.title: Split estate is the rule, not the exception

sections.title: Confirming your patent type before you price anything

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Hot Springs County, WY
items.meta: Hot Springs County, WY mineral owner near Thermopolis and the Hamilton Dome field? Get a fair, no-obligation cash offer for your interest.

sections.html:
Hot Springs County is Wyoming's smallest by population, centered on Thermopolis and its mineral hot springs, but the ground underneath has been producing oil since before most of the county's current residents were born.

Hamilton Dome field, discovered in the 1920s, remains the county's defining piece of oil history, and it's far from alone. Grass Creek, just over the line in Hot Springs and Park counties, and a handful of smaller structural traps have kept this county in the production business for a century, even as the rest of the world knows it mainly for the hot springs and the state's namesake bath house.

If you're holding a mineral interest here, it likely came down through a family that ranched or farmed this ground long before oil was found on it, kept the minerals through an original homestead patent, and has been collecting some form of royalty check, however modest, for longer than anyone currently in the family can remember firsthand.

sections.title: Hamilton Dome and the county's legacy production
sections.html:
Hamilton Dome sits near Kirby and has been re-worked, re-completed, and put through secondary recovery multiple times since its 1920s discovery. It's the kind of field that never made headlines the way the Powder River Basin's horizontal boom did, but it's kept producing at stripper levels through nearly every commodity cycle Wyoming has seen since.

Nearby structures around Lucerne and toward the Big Horn County line share similar geology and similar history, shallow structural traps in Phosphoria and Tensleep-equivalent formations that were among the first targets explored in this part of the Bighorn Basin.

sections.title: Thermopolis, the county seat, and where your records live
sections.html:
Every deed, lease, probate filing, and division order tied to Hot Springs County mineral ownership is recorded at the county clerk's office in Thermopolis. Given the county's small size, that office often has an easier time helping owners track down older or incomplete records than you'd find in a larger, busier county courthouse elsewhere in the state.

That's worth using. If your family's paperwork is thin, missing, or simply confusing after multiple generations of transfers, the clerk's recorded documents are the fastest way to reconstruct exactly what you own before you talk to anyone about selling it.

sections.title: Small county, small interests, real value
sections.html:

Ranchers here have always understood that what's above the ground and what's below it are two different kinds of property. Barnum field and similar legacy structures have produced for decades in this area, alongside newer horizontal targets.

Ranch families throughout Johnson County commonly hold mineral interests that trace back to original homestead patents from the early 1900s, sometimes with minerals reserved when the surface was later sold to a neighboring operation or a new owner. If your family's patent came through that route, you may own the surface without owning what's underneath it, a split estate situation that's common across this part of Wyoming and not a defect in your title, just a different kind of ownership.

Confirming whether your specific tract is privately owned minerals or federally reserved minerals is the single most important step before pricing any interest, since only privately held minerals are yours to sell.

Horizontal wells in this part of the basin typically show a strong first-year decline followed by a longer, flatter stripper-style tail, which means your check five years into a well's life will look very different from your first one, without anything having gone wrong. Buyers price interests against that decline curve, not against your best month.

Bring your most recent two or three check stubs, your division order, and your original mineral deed when you're ready to get a real number instead of a guess. Laramie County sits where the Denver-Julesburg Basin's northern tail reaches into Wyoming, Cheyenne as the county seat, and a mineral history shaped as much by the old Union Pacific railroad grant as by any drilling boom.

The DJ Basin has made fortunes on the Colorado side for years, out of the Niobrara and Codell formations, but the play thins as it crosses into Wyoming, and Laramie County's oil and gas story has always been more modest and more sporadic as a result.

That doesn't mean the mineral estate here isn't real or isn't worth understanding. It means figuring out what you own, and what it's genuinely worth, takes more than assuming your acreage behaves like acreage forty miles south across the state line.

sections.title: How far the DJ Basin trend actually reaches
sections.html:
Reservoir quality in the Niobrara and Codell generally improves toward the basin's structural center, which sits well south of the Wyoming line. Laramie County acreage has drawn leasing interest in waves over the years, periods when operators pushed exploration north to test the play's edge, followed by quieter stretches when interest retreated back toward the Colorado core.

If your family's minerals have been leased before, even if that lease has since expired, it's a sign your specific tract has drawn real operator attention at some point, which matters more to a buyer than acreage that's never seen a landman.

sections.title: The Union Pacific checkerboard along the transcontinental corridor
sections.html:
Southern Laramie County still carries the 1862 Union Pacific railroad land grant pattern in places, alternating odd and even sections that split between private railroad-origin land and federal ground. That checkerboard runs roughly along the historic transcontinental rail corridor and still shapes how mineral ownership and any future unit boundaries get drawn up in this part of the county.

If your legal description sits on one of those odd-numbered sections, your ownership traces to a private patent rather than a federal homestead, which is worth knowing when a landman starts explaining who else might be involved in a potential unit.

sections.title: Cheyenne's growth and old ranch mineral severances
sections.html:
As Cheyenne has grown, ranch and agricultural land on its outskirts has steadily subdivided into residential and commercial development. Mineral rights under a lot of that ground stayed with the original owning family, severed from the surface at the point of sale, which means present-day mineral owners are often scattered far from the actual property, sometimes without knowing exactly what they hold until an estate is settled.

If your family sold land near Cheyenne at some point over the past several decades but kept the minerals, that reservation is likely still recorded and enforceable today, regardless of how many times the surface has changed hands since.

sections.title: What a fair Laramie County offer is built on
sections.html:
For interests with an active lease or production history, current volume, decline trend, and division order details drive the number. For unleased or undeveloped acreage, which describes a meaningful share of Laramie County mineral ownership, the offer is built on proximity to any active DJ Basin leasing activity and general market appetite for speculative northern-tail acreage.

Either way, start with your deed and legal description. The Laramie County Clerk's office in Cheyenne can confirm section, township, and range, along with any lease history recorded against your specific tract, before you commit to a number with anyone.

sections.title: F.E. Warren Air Force Base and mineral development limits
sections.html:
A significant portion of Laramie County's land near Cheyenne falls under or near F.E. Warren Air Force Base, federal military land where private oil and gas development isn't an option regardless of underlying mineral ownership. If your family's paperwork references land in or adjacent to the base boundary, confirming your tract's status relative to that boundary matters before assuming standard county valuation applies.

Outside the base, and outside any confirmed DJ Basin lease activity, most Laramie County mineral interests fall into the same undeveloped, speculative category as much of Star Valley or the Bighorn Basin's quieter corners, real, recorded, and sellable, but priced conservatively against proven production rather than an active royalty stream.

faqs.q: Is the DJ Basin play currently active in Laramie County?
faqs.a: Interest has run in cycles rather than a steady buildout. Check current permit and lease filings through the Laramie County Clerk or the Wyoming Oil and Gas Conservation Commission for your specific section.

faqs.q: What does checkerboard land mean for your mineral ownership?
faqs.a: It reflects the alternating pattern of private railroad-grant sections and federal sections from the 1862 Union Pacific land grant. It shapes who your neighboring owners are and how units get assembled, not your legal right to your own section.

faqs.q: Your family sold the ranch near Cheyenne decades ago, could the family still own the minerals?
faqs.a: Possibly, if the sale document reserved minerals to the seller. Check your family's copy of the deed, or have the Laramie County Clerk pull the recorded document if you don't have it.

faqs.q: Is unleased Laramie County acreage worth selling?
faqs.a: It can be, priced conservatively as speculative acreage tied to the DJ Basin's northern-tail potential rather than as producing minerals.

faqs.q: Does proximity to F.E. Warren Air Force Base affect your mineral rights?
faqs.a: If your tract sits within or adjacent to the base boundary, private oil and gas development is generally not possible there regardless of your underlying ownership. Confirm your legal description against the base boundary through the Laramie County Clerk.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Lincoln County, WY
items.meta: Lincoln County, WY mineral owner near Kemmerer, Star Valley, or the LaBarge gas platform? Get a fair, no-obligation cash offer for your interest.

sections.html:
Lincoln County covers two very different worlds, the Overthrust Belt and Moxa Arch gas country around Kemmerer and LaBarge, and the quiet farming valleys of Star Valley to the west, and what your mineral interest is worth depends heavily on which one you're standing in.

We have worked title on both ends of this county, and the difference is stark. East of the Star Valley divide, deep thrust-faulted structures have produced major gas discoveries for over a century. West of it, in Star Valley proper, mineral rights have mostly sat unleased and undeveloped through the same stretch of time.

Knowing which side of that line your acreage falls on is the single most useful thing you can figure out before pricing your interest.

sections.title: The Overthrust Belt and Moxa Arch, Lincoln County's productive core
sections.html:
The thrust faulting that stacked up gas-bearing reservoirs across eastern Lincoln County created some of Wyoming's most significant deep gas discoveries when explored through the 1970s and 1980s. The Moxa Arch trend, running through the eastern part of the county toward Sweetwater County, has produced steadily from tight Frontier and Dakota sands for decades.

The LaBarge platform, near the town of La Barge, adds another layer, a deep, high-CO2 gas structure with major processing infrastructure that's kept it commercially active since the 1960s. Mineral owners in this eastern band of the county are far more likely to hold producing, leased interests than owners further west.

sections.title: Kemmerer's coal alongside the gas
sections.html: Kemmerer, the county seat, has been a coal town since the 1890s, and some Lincoln County mineral deeds cover coal rights alongside or instead of oil and gas. If your deed uses broad 'all minerals' language, it may include coal even if you've only ever thought of your interest as an oil and gas asset, worth confirming before you assume what you're selling.

sections.title: Star Valley, where the minerals have mostly stayed quiet
sections.html:
West of the Salt River Range, Star Valley's farming and ranching communities, Etna, Fairview, Freedom, Grover, Thayne, and others, sit outside the geology that's made eastern Lincoln County productive. Mineral rights here trace mostly to old homestead and farm-sale severances, held by families who've never seen a lease, let alone a royalty check.

That's not a defect in the asset. It just means valuation on Star Valley acreage runs speculative, priced on the small chance of future interest rather than existing production, and offers should be understood in that light from the start.

sections.title: Getting an accurate number, either side of the county
sections.html:
For eastern Lincoln County interests tied to Moxa Arch or LaBarge platform production, bring your division order and recent check stubs; established, well-documented units make for fast, confident offers. For Star Valley acreage, bring your deed and legal description and expect a more conservative number reflecting undeveloped ground.

The Lincoln County Clerk's office in Kemmerer holds recorded deeds and lease history for the entire county, both sides of the divide, and is the fastest way to confirm exactly what you own before any sale conversation goes further.

sections.title: Fossil Butte and federally managed ground
sections.html:
Fossil Butte National Monument sits near Kemmerer, federal land removed from oil and gas development entirely, a reminder that even in the county's productive eastern half, not every acre is open to leasing. Surrounding BLM-administered land, common throughout eastern Lincoln County, remains open to federal mineral leasing, but that leasing runs through the Bureau of Land Management rather than a private landowner, and produces no benefit to a nearby private mineral owner unless their own tract is directly involved.

Between the monument, BLM ground, and privately held minerals scattered across both the productive east and the quiet Star Valley west, Lincoln County's mineral map is genuinely more layered than most Wyoming counties. Confirming exactly which category your family's specific tract falls into, private and producing, private and undeveloped, or federally managed, is worth doing before you form any expectations about value.

faqs.q: How do you know if your Lincoln County minerals are in the productive eastern part of the county?
faqs.a: Check your legal description's section, township, and range against a county plat map, or ask the Lincoln County Clerk in Kemmerer to help place your tract relative to the Moxa Arch and Overthrust Belt trend.

faqs.q: Does your deed include coal rights near Kemmerer?
faqs.a: Depends on the deed language. Some Lincoln County deeds specify oil and gas only, others use broader 'all minerals' wording covering coal as well.

faqs.q: Is Star Valley mineral acreage worth anything if it's never been leased?
faqs.a: Yes, though it's priced conservatively as speculative rather than producing acreage. Some owners still choose to sell to consolidate an inherited interest into cash.

faqs.q: What is the LaBarge platform and why does it matter for your minerals?
faqs.a: It's a major deep gas field near La Barge with high CO2 content and significant processing infrastructure, active since the 1960s. If your interest ties to that unit, it likely has a well-documented production history.

faqs.q: How much of Lincoln County's minerals are federally owned versus private?
faqs.a: A substantial share, particularly in the eastern part of the county and around Fossil Butte National Monument, is federally managed BLM or National Park Service land. Confirm your specific tract's status through the Lincoln County Clerk before assuming either way.

sections.html:
Little America is best known as the truck stop and travel plaza off I-80, but the land around it sits squarely in Sweetwater County's checkerboard mineral pattern.

This stretch of southern Wyoming, along the historic transcontinental railroad and now I-80, is where the 1862 Union Pacific land grant left its clearest mark on the map, alternating sections of private and federal ownership that still shape mineral rights today.

sections.title: Living in the checkerboard's core
sections.html: If your family's tract near Little America traces to a Union Pacific railroad patent, an odd-numbered section, you likely own the minerals outright alongside the surface. If it traces to a later federal homestead patent, minerals may have been reserved to the government under the Stock-Raising Homestead Act, meaning the BLM owns what's underneath even though you hold the surface.

sections.title: What's been drilled nearby
sections.html: Gas activity tied to the Bridger field and similar Sweetwater County trends has periodically extended into this area. Confirming whether your specific section has ever been leased takes a records check, not a guess based on what you can see from I-80.

sections.title: Selling checkerboard-pattern minerals
sections.html: First confirm whether you actually own the minerals, private patent or federal reservation, then gather your legal description and any lease history. Sweetwater County Clerk records in Green River hold both patent and lease history for this stretch of the county.

sections.title: Why the travel plaza doesn't define the mineral picture
sections.html: Little America's fame as an I-80 stop has nothing to do with the mineral estate underneath the surrounding sections, which follows the same checkerboard patent history as any other tract in this part of Sweetwater County. Don't let the roadside landmark distract from what actually matters: your legal description and patent type.

sections.title: Build the County-Record Packet
sections.html: A town name is only the first line of a Wyoming mineral file. The working packet should connect the tract to the county, legal description, section, township, range, owner name, vesting instrument, reservations, lease, division order, payor record, and any probate or trust document that changed the chain. Local field history belongs beside the recorded evidence, not in place of it. Where fee minerals meet federal or state ownership, the packet should also identify which tract, depth, or formation is actually private and conveyable before any acreage or paid decimal is carried into an offer.

sections.title: Keep the Paid Interest and the Deed Scope Aligned
sections.html: A royalty statement can show what is being paid on a tract, but the statement does not by itself prove the full mineral estate. The review should reconcile the paid decimal to the ownership fraction, lease royalty, unit allocation, well, product, production month, deductions, taxes, suspense, and any adjustment line. The proposed deed and written purchase scope should then repeat the verified owner, county, legal description, included depths or formations, effective date, conveyed fraction, retained interest, pre-closing proceeds, title conditions, and recording instructions. Any mismatch stays on the curative list until the supporting record resolves it.

faqs.q: Do you own the minerals under your Little America-area land?
faqs.a: It depends on whether your patent traces to the Union Pacific railroad grant or a federal homestead. Check with the Sweetwater County Clerk or BLM records to confirm.

faqs.q: What is the Bridger field and does it reach your tract?
faqs.a: It's a Sweetwater County tight-gas trend. Whether it reaches your specific section requires checking current lease and unit filings for your legal description.

faqs.q: Can you sell minerals if the BLM owns them instead of you?
faqs.a: No, you can only sell what you actually own. If your minerals were federally reserved, you'd have nothing to sell regardless of surface ownership.

faqs.q: Does commercial development near Little America affect nearby mineral value?
faqs.a: Not directly. Mineral value ties to production status, lease history, and geology, not to surface commercial activity like the travel plaza.

sections.title: Multi-generation farm families and mineral memory

items.meta: Own minerals under Salt Creek, the North Platte breaks, or a Powder River flank tract in Natrona County? Get a straight offer from a working landman.

sections.html:
Casper is the county seat, and Natrona County has been oil country since before Wyoming was a state. If you hold minerals here, there is almost always a record of them at the courthouse.

Natrona County sits where the old Salt Creek field runs into the southern edge of the Powder River Basin, with the North Platte River cutting the county in half on its way past Casper. This is some of the oldest production in the Rocky Mountains. Salt Creek was drilled before 1910 and is still pumping stripper wells today, mostly shallow Wall Creek and Frontier sand. North and east of Casper, operators have chased Niobrara and Turner Sand horizontals down toward the Converse County line, and some of those units reach back into Natrona.

What that means for a mineral owner is two very different kinds of interest can sit in the same county. Some families hold small legacy fractions under Salt Creek that have paid a modest, steady royalty for generations. Others hold flank acreage that only got interesting once horizontal rigs started walking north out of Converse. We work both kinds, and we do not treat a five-dollar-a-month legacy interest the same as an active unit — the file work is different and so is the offer.

sections.title: Salt Creek legacy interests
sections.html:
A lot of what crosses our desk out of Natrona County traces back to Salt Creek allotments split up decades ago. Original 40s and 80s got carved into eighths and sixteenths as they passed through estates, and by now some owners have interests measured in the thousandths. The wells are old, mostly stripper production on artificial lift, and the decline curve flattened out a long time ago. That is not a knock on the interest — a flat, long-lived stripper royalty can be worth selling precisely because it is predictable, and predictable is what a buyer can price without guessing.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Sublette County, WY
items.meta: Minerals under the Jonah Field or Pinedale Anticline in Sublette County? Get an offer priced against the real spacing and BLM checkerboard on your tract.

sections.html:
Pinedale is the county seat, and Sublette County sits over two of the biggest gas fields in the Rocky Mountains — Jonah and the Pinedale Anticline. Few counties in Wyoming have a tighter link between mineral ownership and the federal checkerboard.

Sublette County is Green River Basin gas country, tight sand production out of the Lance and Mesaverde formations, developed on close well spacing across the Jonah Field and the Pinedale Anticline. Both fields were built out under federal environmental review with directional drilling from consolidated pads, which changed how spacing units get drawn compared to older Wyoming fields. If you hold minerals here, there is a good chance your tract sits inside a formally established federal unit with a specific participating area, not a loosely bounded old-style spacing unit.

This county is also where the Union Pacific checkerboard runs thickest through active development. The railroad grant gave UP the odd-numbered sections in a mile-wide band on either side of the original transcontinental route, and much of that land was later sold off with the minerals going a dozen different directions — while the even sections stayed federal, with BLM administering the minerals underneath. On a map of Jonah or the Anticline, that checkerboard pattern is why two neighboring sections can have completely different ownership rules, and why title work here takes real care.

sections.title: The checkerboard and split estate in Sublette County
sections.html: Because of the Union Pacific land grant, a lot of Sublette County alternates between federal BLM sections and private sections that trace back to old railroad patents. Where the surface was sold off private but minerals were reserved by the railroad or a later owner, you get split estate — someone else owns the surface a rig sits on, and you own what's underneath. County clerk records in Pinedale, combined with BLM's Wyoming state office records for the federal sections, are how we confirm which pattern applies to your tract before we quote a number.

sections.title: Jonah Field and the tight-sand decline curve
sections.html: Jonah is one of the more heavily developed tight gas fields in the country, drilled on close spacing to drain a low-permeability reservoir that does not flow easily without a lot of wellbores. That means individual well decline curves are steep early and flatten out over years, and a mineral owner's royalty stream reflects that shape — strong in the first few years after completion, then settling into a longer tail. If your interest is inside the Jonah participating area, we look at where in that curve current production sits before pricing an offer.

sections.title: What drives the offer here
sections.html: Sublette County pricing leans heavily on which field your acreage sits in, how deep into the well's productive life the current royalty checks reflect, and whether your tract is inside an established federal participating area or still speculative acreage on the fringe. Gas price swings hit this county's royalty checks more directly than an oil county, since almost all of the production here is Lance and Mesaverde gas rather than oil, so we look at a longer stretch of your payment history than we might elsewhere to smooth out any one bad month.

sections.title: The Pinedale Anticline and directional development
sections.html: The Anticline was developed later than Jonah and mostly from consolidated well pads using directional drilling, which was required to limit surface disturbance in mule deer and sage grouse habitat. For a mineral owner, that means your tract may be drained by a wellbore that surfaces from a pad a half mile or more away — the well location on a map is not where your minerals actually sit. We trace bottom-hole locations against your legal description before making an offer, not only surface locations.

faqs.q: How do you know if your minerals are inside the Jonah Field or the Pinedale Anticline participating area?
faqs.a: Your division order will usually name the unit or participating area directly. If you only have an old lease, send us the legal description and we can check it against BLM and Wyoming Oil and Gas Conservation Commission unit records.

faqs.q: Your section is federal BLM land — do you even own minerals there?
faqs.a: If the section is federal, the government owns the minerals, not you. But a lot of Sublette County acreage is privately owned minerals in odd-numbered sections tied to the old railroad grant, so it depends on which section your legal description falls in.

faqs.q: Why does the well on the map look nowhere near your tract?
faqs.a: Anticline development uses directional drilling from consolidated pads, so a well can be bottomed under your section while surfacing somewhere else entirely. We check bottom-hole location, not only the surface pin, before pricing your interest.

faqs.q: Gas prices swing a lot — how does that affect what you'll offer?
faqs.a: We look at a run of recent royalty history rather than a single check, so a short-term price dip doesn't distort the number. We'll walk you through how we weighted it.

faqs.q: Do you buy interests that are still in the leasing stage but not yet producing?
faqs.a: We look at those case by case, weighted on how close the acreage is to established production in Jonah or the Anticline and whether permits are already filed nearby.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Sweetwater County, WY
items.meta: Minerals in the Green River Basin's biggest county — trona, tight gas, or Wamsutter oil? Get an offer that accounts for what's actually under your tract.

sections.html:
Green River is the county seat, and Sweetwater County is the largest in Wyoming by land area — a stretch of tight gas fields, trona beds, and checkerboard railroad ground running from Rock Springs east to Wamsutter.

Sweetwater County covers more ground than some states, and the mineral picture changes as you cross it. Around Rock Springs and Green River, you have a mix of Fort Union and Mesaverde gas production layered over some of the largest trona deposits in the world — trona being the raw material for soda ash, mined here on a scale most people outside Wyoming never hear about. East toward Wamsutter, the geology shifts into tight oil and gas in the Almond and Lewis formations, developed on close-spaced units similar to what you see across the border in the Great Divide Basin.

The other constant across the whole county is the checkerboard. The original Union Pacific transcontinental grant runs straight through Sweetwater County, alternating odd federal-adjacent private sections with even BLM sections mile by mile. That pattern, more than almost anywhere else in the state, decides who you deal with, what paperwork exists, and how fast a sale can close.

sections.title: Rock Springs and Green River — gas, trona, and old title
sections.html: The Rock Springs uplift has produced natural gas for decades, and much of the acreage around the city has been drilled and re-drilled as completion technology improved. Layered underneath a lot of that same ground is trona, mined by several companies for soda ash production — a mineral interest here can theoretically involve both oil and gas rights and solid mineral (trona) rights, and those are sometimes severed from each other separately, not only from the surface. Before we make an offer on acreage in this part of the county, we confirm exactly which mineral category your deed actually conveys.

sections.title: Wamsutter and the tight gas fairway
sections.html: East toward Wamsutter, the county sits over some of the most heavily developed tight gas acreage in the Rockies, close-spaced units targeting the Almond, Lewis, and Fort Union intervals. Wells here decline fast and get infilled aggressively, so a royalty history from five years ago does not tell you much about what the interest is worth today. We weight recent months heavily when pricing acreage in this part of the county rather than relying on an older average.

sections.title: The checkerboard and split estate
sections.html: Because the Union Pacific grant runs the length of the county, a huge share of Sweetwater County's private mineral ownership traces back to railroad patents on odd-numbered sections, with the even sections remaining federal and administered by the BLM Rock Springs field office. Surface use agreements, access, and even which regulator has jurisdiction can flip section to section. If your family's minerals came down through a ranch that straddled that pattern, split estate is common — the rancher who owned the surface often was not the same party who ended up with the minerals a generation or two later.

sections.title: Pricing across a county this size
sections.html: There is no single number that works for Sweetwater County — a trona-adjacent gas interest near Rock Springs, a fast-declining Wamsutter unit, and a quiet legacy fraction in between all price differently. We start with your division order or legal description, confirm the mineral type and the specific unit, and check recent production filed with the Wyoming Oil and Gas Conservation Commission before we ever put a number in front of you.

faqs.q: Your deed mentions oil, gas, and 'other minerals' — does that include the trona under Rock Springs?
faqs.a: It depends on the exact language and how the interest was originally severed. Some deeds cover solid minerals like trona, others don't. We read the deed language carefully before we price anything in that part of the county.

faqs.q: Why does your Wamsutter royalty check jump around so much?
faqs.a: Tight gas wells in that part of the county decline quickly and get infilled with new wells fairly often, so production and pricing both move. We look at a recent stretch of checks rather than one snapshot.

faqs.q: How do you find out if your section is BLM federal or private railroad-grant land?
faqs.a: Your legal description tells us. Odd-numbered sections in the historic railroad grant band are typically the private ones; even sections are usually federal. We confirm it against BLM Rock Springs field office and county clerk records.

faqs.q: Is Sweetwater County a good place to sell, or should you hold and keep collecting royalty?
faqs.a: That depends on your situation and risk tolerance — we're not going to tell you what's right for your finances. What we can do is give you a real, current offer so you have an actual number to weigh against holding.

faqs.q: What paperwork do you need to get started?
faqs.a: A division order or recent check stub is fastest. If you only have an old lease, mineral deed, or probate record, send what you have and we'll trace the rest through the courthouse in Green River.

The Almond and Lewis formations underlying Wamsutter have been drilled on close spacing for decades, and infill drilling has continued to add wells to units that were already developed years earlier. That density is the defining feature of a Wamsutter mineral interest — your tract may sit inside a unit with far more wellbores than a typical Wyoming spacing unit, and the royalty history reflects a lot of individual well declines layered on top of each other.
