items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Warren AFB, WY
items.meta: Own minerals under the ranch ground around F.E. Warren AFB in Laramie County? We buy DJ Basin mineral and royalty interests. Free courthouse-checked offer.

sections.html:
The base itself sits on federal ground, but the ranch land that surrounds it went to homestead patent generations ago, and that's where the mineral interests we buy actually sit.

F.E. Warren Air Force Base has occupied this ground west of Cheyenne since 1867, and the installation itself doesn't carry private mineral rights - the federal government holds what's under the fence line. What we work is the land around it: the old ranch sections along the Laramie County line that got patented out under the Homestead Act and later the 1862 railroad grant, then passed down through families for a hundred and fifty years.

Laramie County sits on the northern edge of the DJ Basin, the same Niobrara and Codell trend that's been active south into Colorado. It's not the drilling density you see closer to the Colorado line, but the mineral interests are real, they're recorded at the Laramie County Clerk's office in Cheyenne, and plenty of them are still held in small fractional shares by heirs who've never set foot on the property.

sections.title: Why Ownership Here Looks the Way It Does
sections.html:
The Union Pacific's original transcontinental grant ran straight through this part of Laramie County - odd-numbered sections to the railroad, even to the federal government, the classic Wyoming checkerboard. Warren AFB itself was withdrawn from that pattern early and went military. But drive a few miles off base and you're back in the checkerboard, ranch land bought up from the railroad or homesteaded on the government sections, minerals frequently severed from the surface at some point along the way.

That severance history is the whole reason a title search matters before anyone signs anything. A family that's ranched the same quarter section since the 1930s might hold full mineral rights, or they might hold none, with a distant cousin's estate controlling a sliver interest instead.

sections.title: What We're Actually Buying
sections.html:
Non-producing mineral interests in Laramie County near the base, small fractional shares inherited from a ranch estate, and old royalty interests tied to DJ Basin activity to the south and east. Most of what comes across our desk here is undeveloped or lightly held - no active well, just a mineral deed sitting in a family file since the 1960s.

We also look at interests complicated by probate, where heirs in three states can't agree on next steps and nobody wants to keep tracking a county tax notice for ground they've never seen.

sections.title: How the Offer Gets Built
sections.html: We pull the deed history at the Laramie County Clerk's office in Cheyenne, confirm your net mineral acreage against the legal description, and check DJ Basin activity trends before we put a number in front of you. If there's no production history, that offer reflects speculative value tied to basin activity, not a guaranteed payout - we say that plainly, because anyone promising you a locked-in price without checking the record first isn't being straight with you.

faqs.q: Do you own minerals if your land borders Warren AFB?
faqs.a: The base itself holds federal mineral rights under the installation, but land adjoining it is private, and mineral ownership there depends entirely on the deed and severance history for that specific parcel. We check the record before we say anything definitive.

faqs.q: Is there active drilling near Warren AFB?
faqs.a: This part of Laramie County sits on the northern flank of the DJ Basin, well behind the core Niobrara activity further south. Values here typically reflect basin-wide trends rather than an active well on the lease.

faqs.q: Your mineral interest came from a family ranch estate. Can you still buy it?
faqs.a: Yes. Estate-derived fractional interests are common in this county, and we work directly with heirs, including cases where the interest hasn't been formally probated yet.

faqs.q: How do you value an undeveloped mineral interest here?
faqs.a: We weigh net mineral acres, DJ Basin activity trends, and any historical lease or royalty data tied to the tract. Undeveloped interests get a range tied to that activity, not a fixed promise.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Washakie County, WY
items.meta: Own oil, gas, or mineral rights in Washakie County, WY? We buy Bighorn Basin mineral interests around Worland and Ten Sleep. Free courthouse-checked offer.

sections.html:
Washakie County has been producing oil out of the Bighorn Basin since before Wyoming had paved highways, and a lot of what's under the ground here is still held the way it was left by the original homestead patents.

Washakie County sits in the middle of the Bighorn Basin, bounded by the Bighorn Mountains to the east and the Absarokas out west, with the Nowood River cutting through the southern part of the county on its way to join the Bighorn. Worland is the county seat, and the courthouse there holds the deed and probate records for just about every mineral interest tied to this ground going back to statehood-era homesteads.

This isn't a boomtown county. It's a working basin with a long production history, small towns, ranch families who've held the same section for four or five generations, and a courthouse staff that's used to pulling mineral deed books for people who moved away decades ago and still hold an interest their grandfather never sold.

sections.title: The Geology Under Washakie County
sections.html:
The Bighorn Basin is layered oil country - the Tensleep Sandstone, named for the town just west of Worland, has been a workhorse producing zone across the basin for a hundred years. Below it sits the Phosphoria, and deeper still the Madison Limestone, both of which have paid off in various fields across the county over the decades. Shallower Cretaceous and Cloverly zones round out the picture on the flanks.

Washakie County's own production history runs through fields like Big Sand Draw and Winkleman Dome, structural traps that were found early in the basin's development and have been producing, declining, and getting re-worked in cycles ever since. It's mature basin behavior - steady decline curves, periodic re-entry and workover activity, not the sharp production spikes you'd see out of an unconventional shale play.

sections.title: How Ownership Broke Up Here
sections.html:
Most of Washakie County's mineral ownership traces back to homestead patents from the early 1900s, when ranch families proved up 160 or 320 acre tracts along the Nowood and around the irrigated bottomland near Worland and Ten Sleep. Minerals often stayed with the surface at first, then got severed off in a lease or sale sometime in the 1930s through the 1950s as oil activity picked up in the basin.

What that means today is a lot of fractional ownership. A single quarter section might have eight or ten mineral owners on record, heirs of heirs, some still local, most scattered to Colorado, Montana, or further. Washakie County isn't checkerboard country the way southern Wyoming along the old Union Pacific grant is, but there's still meaningful federal minerals mixed with private ground here, tied to BLM administration rather than railroad grant history, which affects who you'd even lease with on a given tract.

Because the county's oil history is so long, it's also common to find mineral deeds with outdated legal descriptions, old unit designations that don't match how a tract is described today, or royalty interests that were carved out of a larger family estate and never cleanly re-recorded. None of that stops a sale, but it does mean the title work takes an actual look at the Washakie County Clerk's records rather than a rubber stamp.

sections.title: Towns and Ground We Work Across the County
sections.html:
Worland anchors the county as both the seat and the population center, sitting on the Bighorn River with the courthouse, the clerk's office, and most of the county's services. Ten Sleep, up against the base of the Bighorn Mountains along the old stage route, gave its name to the Tensleep Sandstone and still has ranch families holding minerals from the original homestead era. Manderson and Hyattville round out the smaller communities, both closer to the basin's edge where production has historically been thinner but not absent.

We buy interests across all of it - producing royalty tied to a Tensleep well that's been paying small checks for decades, non-producing acreage that's never seen a rig, and fractional interests split among heirs who mostly just want the county tax notice and the annual division order paperwork to stop showing up.

sections.title: What Selling Actually Involves
sections.html:
We start with the deed record at the Washakie County Clerk's office in Worland, confirm your net mineral acreage and legal description against what's actually recorded, and check current activity and historical production on the tract before we build a number. If there's an active royalty history, we look at the decline curve rather than just the last few checks, since a well three years into decline pays differently than one that's five years past its peak.

If you're an heir dealing with a fractional interest that's never been cleanly divided, we can usually work through that without forcing a full formal partition. Value talk here is always a range tied to production and basin activity - nobody selling minerals in a mature basin like this should be hearing a locked-in guaranteed number before the record's been checked.

faqs.q: Is Washakie County part of the Bighorn Basin checkerboard?
faqs.a: No, the classic Wyoming checkerboard comes from the Union Pacific's railroad grant across southern counties like Sweetwater and Carbon. Washakie County has its own mix of private and federal minerals, tied more to BLM administration and original homestead patents than to railroad grant history.

faqs.q: What's the Tensleep Sandstone and why does it matter for your mineral rights?
faqs.a: It's a major producing formation named for the town of Ten Sleep, and it's been the workhorse zone for Bighorn Basin oil production for a century. If your interest is in Washakie County, there's a good chance any historical production on it came from the Tensleep or the Phosphoria beneath it.

faqs.q: Where are mineral deeds and probate records kept for this county?
faqs.a: At the Washakie County Clerk's office in Worland, the county seat. That's where we start every title check before making an offer.

faqs.q: You inherited a fractional mineral interest with several other heirs. Can you buy just your share?
faqs.a: Yes. We regularly buy individual heir shares without requiring the whole family group to sell together or forcing a formal court partition.

faqs.a: Sometimes. A shut-in or plugged well can still leave the underlying mineral interest worth something if the tract has re-entry or offset potential, but we evaluate that on the specific well and formation rather than assuming.

Washam is a rail siding, not a town with a courthouse of its own - your mineral rights here run through Sweetwater County records in Green River, and the section lines still follow the old railroad pattern.

Washam sits out in the open country of southern Sweetwater County, the kind of place that shows up on a plat map more than it does on a highway sign. There's no town government to speak of, but the ground underneath has been part of the Green River Basin's oil, gas, and trona story for close to a century.

This is core Union Pacific checkerboard territory. The original 1862 railroad grant handed the UP the odd-numbered sections in a strip across southern Wyoming, and the pattern is still stamped on every plat around Washam - private and federal sections alternating like a checkerboard, which is exactly what the old-timers call it. Whoever holds your mineral deed inherited that pattern whether they know it or not.

sections.title: The Green River Basin Around Washam
sections.html:
Sweetwater County is Green River Basin bedrock - tight gas out of the Lance and Fort Union, deeper Frontier and Almond production, and a legacy of Wamsutter-area drilling that stretches back decades. Washam itself sits removed from the densest activity around Wamsutter and Table Rock, but it's inside the basin's broader productive fairway, and lease interest here tracks basin-wide gas prices more than any single well.

Add to that Sweetwater's trona beds - the county produces most of the nation's soda ash - and you've got a place where mineral ownership sometimes means more than oil and gas. If your deed language is broad ('all minerals'), it's worth checking whether it reaches the trona horizon too.

We run the deed history at the Sweetwater County Clerk's office in Green River before we quote anything, because the legal description on an old family mineral deed doesn't always match current section lines cleanly.

faqs.a: No. Washam is an unincorporated place in Sweetwater County. Deed and title records for property here are filed at the Sweetwater County Clerk's office in Green River.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Wright, WY
items.meta: Own mineral rights near Wright, WY in the Powder River Basin? We buy coal-adjacent and CBM/oil mineral interests. Deed history checked before any offer.

sections.html:
Wright was built by ARCO as a company town to run the coal mines around it, and mineral ownership out here is almost never simple - coal, coalbed methane, and conventional oil and gas can sit under the same section held by three different owners.

Wright came up in the 1970s as a planned town to support the Black Thunder and Jacobs Ranch mine operations, and Campbell County around it has been the single largest coal-producing county in the country for decades. But coal isn't the only thing under this ground - the same acreage has coalbed methane history from the CBM boom of the late 1990s and 2000s, and conventional Powder River Basin oil zones sit deeper still.

That layering is exactly why mineral ownership here is rarely one clean deed. It's common to find the coal severed to one party, oil and gas rights held separately by another, and a small legacy CBM royalty interest from the boom years sitting on top of both, all tied to the same quarter section.

sections.title: Coal, CBM, and Split Estate Around Wright
sections.html:
A lot of Campbell County coal is federally owned and leased through BLM competitive coal leasing, which means the surface rancher, the coal mineral owner, and the oil and gas mineral owner can be three entirely different parties on the same tract. If your family homesteaded ranch ground here, there's a real chance you kept the oil and gas rights even if the coal underneath was already federal, or reserved separately generations ago.

The CBM boom left its own mark. Wells drilled in the late 1990s through the mid-2000s across the Powder River Basin dewatered coal seams to release methane, and a lot of those wells have gone through steep decline or been plugged entirely as the boom went bust. If you're holding a royalty interest from that era, the check you're getting now, if you're getting one at all, is likely a fraction of what it was fifteen years ago.

sections.title: What Owning Minerals Near Wright Usually Means
sections.html: Most private mineral interests we see around Wright trace back to ranch homesteads that predate the town itself, with rights split off through a coal lease, an oil and gas lease, or both at different points. Some owners hold only the oil and gas, with coal already tied up under federal lease. Others hold a small legacy CBM royalty that barely moves the needle anymore but still generates a check and a tax form every year.

sections.title: How We Approach an Offer Here
sections.html: We start by sorting out exactly what estate you hold - oil and gas, coal, or both - since Campbell County split estate isn't unusual and it changes the whole valuation. If there's CBM or conventional oil royalty history, we look at the actual decline curve rather than the last check amount, because post-boom CBM interests especially can look deceiving if you only glance at recent numbers. Any offer we give reflects that real production trend, not a flat guess.

faqs.q: Do you own coal, oil and gas, or both under your land near Wright?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on your deed history. Split estate is common in Campbell County, and we sort out exactly what you hold before making any offer.

faqs.q: Your coalbed methane royalty checks have dropped a lot over the years. Is the interest still worth anything?
faqs.a: Often yes, though typically less than during the CBM boom years. We look at your current decline curve rather than assuming based on peak-era numbers.

faqs.q: Is federal BLM coal leasing the same as your private oil and gas rights?
faqs.a: No, they're usually separate. Federal coal leasing in Campbell County doesn't affect privately held oil and gas minerals under the same tract unless your specific deed says otherwise.

faqs.q: How do you value an interest with mixed coal, CBM, and conventional history?
faqs.a: We evaluate each mineral estate you actually hold separately, weighing production history and current activity for that specific right rather than lumping everything into one number.

situations.title: Owner Situations

items.name: Inherited Mineral Rights
items.meta: Just inherited Wyoming mineral rights and not sure what you own or what it's worth? We help heirs sort the deed history and make a fair cash offer.

sections.html:
Most of the mineral interests we buy in this state didn't start with the seller. They started with a grandparent's homestead patent and landed on a desk sixty or eighty years later with a stack of unfamiliar paperwork.

Inheriting mineral rights usually comes with more questions than answers. There's a deed, maybe a lease from decades ago, maybe a royalty check that's been showing up in a relative's mailbox for years, and now it's yours along with the job of figuring out what any of it means.

You don't have to become an expert in oil and gas to make a good decision here. You need to know what you actually own, whether it's producing, and what it's realistically worth, and then decide whether keeping it or selling it fits your situation better.

sections.title: Figuring Out What You Actually Own
sections.html:
The starting point is the county clerk and recorder's office in whatever county the minerals sit in — Campbell, Sublette, Sweetwater, Laramie, or wherever the deed points. That office has the deed that transferred the minerals to your relative, any lease that's been filed against the property, and the probate or transfer-on-death paperwork that moved it to you.

If your relative passed without a will, or the estate was never formally probated, that step can take longer, because Wyoming law has specific requirements for clearing title through intestate succession. We deal with this regularly and can tell you fairly quickly what's missing and what it would take to fix, without charging you for the diagnosis.

sections.title: Producing, Once-Producing, or Never Drilled
sections.html:
Some inherited interests come with an active royalty check already arriving, which makes valuation more straightforward because there's real payment history to work from. Others produced years ago, went dry or the lease expired, and now sit quiet. Others never had a well drilled at all, just an old reservation sitting in a county that's seen activity nearby.

All three situations have real value, just different kinds. A producing interest is worth its remaining production stream. A once-producing tract is worth its potential for a new well nearby. Undeveloped acreage is worth its position relative to current basin activity. We price all three, and we'll tell you honestly which category yours falls into before we make an offer.

sections.title: Keep It or Sell It
sections.html:
Some heirs want to hold onto family minerals as a connection to the land or a long-term asset, and that's a completely reasonable choice, especially for a producing interest generating steady income. Other heirs live out of state, have no interest in oil and gas as a business, or would rather have the cash to pay down debt, cover a large expense, or split fairly among siblings without managing a shared asset forever.

There's no wrong answer here. We're not going to pressure you toward selling if keeping the interest makes more sense for your family. What we can do is give you a real number, so whichever choice you make, you're making it with actual information instead of a guess.

sections.title: If Multiple Heirs Are Involved
sections.html:
It's common for a single interest to pass to two, three, or more siblings or cousins jointly. You don't all have to agree on what to do. Some heirs can choose to sell their share while others keep theirs, and we handle that split ownership regularly without requiring a unanimous family decision.

If the family does want to sell together, we can put together a single offer covering everyone's share and coordinate the paperwork so each heir signs their own portion, which is usually simpler than it sounds once the title work is done.

sections.title: Old Paperwork Is More Useful Than It Looks
sections.html:
Families often assume that a faded deed, a decades-old lease, or a handwritten note about the property isn't useful because it's incomplete or hard to read. In our experience it's almost always worth more than starting from nothing, because it points us toward the right county, the right section, and sometimes the right original operator, all of which speeds up the records search considerably.

If you genuinely have nothing on paper, that's fine too. A family name, a rough sense of which part of the state the property is in, or even a memory of a relative mentioning oil money is enough for us to start looking.

faqs.q: The estate was never probated. Can the heirs still sell?
faqs.a: It depends on your specific situation, but Wyoming has procedures for clearing title through intestate succession or small estate affidavits in some cases. We can look at what you have and explain what's needed.

faqs.q: How do you find out what county your inherited minerals are in?
faqs.a: Check the original deed if you have it, or any old lease or division order paperwork. If you're not sure, send us whatever documents exist and we can help trace it.

faqs.q: Is it better to sell right after inheriting, or wait?
faqs.a: There's no universal answer. Waiting doesn't automatically increase value, and it can mean more years of managing paperwork on a small interest. We can walk through your specific situation so you decide with real numbers.

faqs.q: Your siblings and you inherited jointly and don't all agree on selling. What now?
faqs.a: Each heir can typically choose independently. We can buy one sibling's share while others keep theirs, so disagreement within the family doesn't have to hold up anyone's decision.

faqs.q: Do you owe taxes on inherited minerals if you sell?
faqs.a: Possibly, depending on your basis and the sale price. Talk to your CPA or tax advisor about your specific situation before you finalize a sale.

items.name: Got an Unsolicited Offer?
items.meta: A letter showed up offering to buy your Wyoming minerals out of nowhere. Before you sign, get a second opinion and a competing written offer from us.

sections.html:
A letter shows up out of nowhere offering to buy minerals you may have forgotten you owned. Before you sign anything, it's worth knowing whether that number is fair.

Unsolicited mineral offers land in Wyoming mailboxes for a reason — someone pulled county records, found your name on a deed, and decided your interest was worth pursuing. That alone tells you something: whoever sent that letter thinks your minerals are worth the cost of tracking you down and making an offer. The question is whether the number they wrote down reflects real value or the lowest figure they thought you might accept.

We're not going to tell you every mailbox offer is a lowball. Some are reasonable. But you have no way to know which kind you've received without a second opinion, and a landman writing offers at volume has no obligation to tell you if they're leaving money on the table.

sections.title: Why Companies Send Offers Sight Unseen
sections.html:
Buyers who mail unsolicited offers are typically working from a list — county mineral ownership records, tax rolls, or probate filings — and sending the same offer format to many owners at once. That's an efficient way for them to find sellers, but it also means the offer is often a starting number rather than a carefully researched valuation of your specific tract, formation, and production history.

Some offers are calculated with real data behind them. Others are set low deliberately, on the assumption that a percentage of recipients will sign without checking, and the ones who do sign subsidize the deals that would have been fair anyway. There's no way to tell which type you've received just by reading the letter.

sections.title: What to Check Before You Sign Anything
sections.html:
Look at whether the letter references your actual production history, lease terms, or just a flat number per net mineral acre with no supporting detail. A real valuation usually explains itself; a mass-mailed offer often doesn't. Also check the deadline — legitimate offers don't usually expire in a way designed to rush you past the point of getting a second opinion.

It's also worth checking whether the offer is for your full interest or a term interest, and whether it includes both mineral and royalty rights or just one. Some unsolicited offers are written in a way that's technically accurate but easy to misread quickly, especially if you're not used to the terminology.

sections.title: Getting a Competing Number
sections.html:
Send us the same legal description or deed information the other offer references, along with a copy of the letter itself if you're comfortable sharing it. We'll pull the same county records, look at what we know about the play and formation your minerals sit in, and give you our own written offer for comparison.

There's no cost or obligation in getting a second number. If our offer comes in lower, we'll tell you that honestly rather than trying to talk you out of the other one. If it comes in higher, you'll have real leverage either to sell to us or to go back to the original party and ask them to match it.

sections.title: There's Usually No Real Rush
sections.html:
Most unsolicited offers include a response deadline, but your minerals aren't going anywhere, and a legitimate buyer's interest in them typically doesn't evaporate in a week or two. If a letter is pressuring you to sign fast without time to check the number, that pressure itself is worth being skeptical of.

Take the time to get a comparison. It costs you nothing and a few days' delay, and it's the only way to know whether the offer sitting on your kitchen table is a fair one or a number set low on purpose.

sections.title: What a Real Second Opinion Looks Like
sections.html:
A credible second opinion should reference your actual acreage, county, and, where it exists, production or lease history, not simply restate a flat per-acre figure back at you. It should also explain the reasoning, so you can judge for yourself whether the logic holds up rather than just comparing two unexplained numbers side by side.

That's the standard we hold ourselves to when we respond to someone who's received an unsolicited offer elsewhere. If we can't beat the number you were sent, we'll tell you plainly instead of manufacturing a competing figure just to win the deal.

faqs.q: Is it normal to receive a mineral rights offer you never asked for?
faqs.a: Yes. Buyers regularly work from county ownership and tax records to identify and contact mineral owners directly, without any prior relationship.

faqs.q: How do you know if the offer you received is fair?
faqs.a: The most reliable way is to get a second, independent offer based on the same legal description and compare the two. We're happy to provide one at no cost.

faqs.q: Does getting a second opinion cost anything?
faqs.a: No. We'll review your legal description and any paperwork you share and provide a written comparison offer with no obligation to proceed.

faqs.q: The offer you got has a tight deadline. Should you worry about missing it?
faqs.a: Most mineral interests aren't time-sensitive in that way. A short deadline designed to rush a decision is itself a reason to slow down and get a comparison first.

faqs.q: Can you go back to the original buyer and negotiate if you get a better offer elsewhere?
faqs.a: Often yes. Having a documented competing offer gives you real leverage to ask the original party to match or explain their number.

items.name: Out-of-State Owners
items.meta: Live outside Wyoming but own minerals here? We buy interests from absentee owners entirely by mail and phone, no trip to a county courthouse required.

sections.html:
You don't have to live in Wyoming, or ever have, to hold minerals here, and you don't have to fly in to sell them either. We close with owners in every part of the country by mail and phone.

A surprising share of Wyoming mineral owners have never set foot in the county where their interest sits. The minerals passed down from a relative who homesteaded or ranched here generations ago, and the family scattered to other states while the interest stayed on the books in Campbell, Sublette, Sweetwater, Laramie, or wherever the original deed was filed.

That distance creates real friction. Royalty checks get mailed to an outdated address. Lease offers arrive by certified mail with a deadline and nobody local to ask about them. Property tax notices, if applicable, go to a forwarding address that eventually stops working. None of that is your fault, but it's the kind of thing that piles up when the asset and the owner are a thousand miles apart.

sections.title: Managing a Wyoming Interest From Somewhere Else
sections.html:
There's no requirement that a mineral owner live near the property, and plenty of Wyoming production is owned by people in Texas, California, the Midwest, and everywhere in between. But managing it well from a distance means staying current on operator changes, keeping your mailing address updated with every company that might send a division order, and tracking lease offers that show up unpredictably.

Most absentee owners we talk to have fallen behind on at least one of those, usually not from neglect but because there was never a clear reason to prioritize it. A check for forty dollars a month doesn't usually justify the time it would take to fully understand what you own and what it's worth.

sections.title: Selling Without Traveling to Wyoming
sections.html:
We handle the entire process by mail, phone, and email. You don't need to visit the county courthouse yourself — we pull the title records directly. You don't need to meet in person to sign; closing documents can be notarized wherever you live and returned by mail. We've closed with sellers who've never seen the acreage their family has owned for eighty years, and that's completely normal.

The one thing that speeds this up on your end is having whatever paperwork you do have handy — an old deed, a royalty statement, a lease, even a family letter that mentions the property. If you don't have any of that, the county and a rough sense of where the property is located is usually enough for us to start.

sections.title: Why Out-of-State Owners Often Choose to Sell
sections.html:
For owners who never plan to live near the minerals or get more involved in managing them, converting a distant, low-touch asset into a single payment is often more useful than continuing to track small checks and occasional mail from operators you've never spoken with. It's one less thing tied to a state you may have no other connection to anymore.

That's not the right call for everyone. Some absentee owners are happy holding a producing interest as passive income regardless of distance. We're not going to push you toward selling if the current arrangement works fine for your family. We just make sure distance itself isn't the reason a fair transaction doesn't happen.

sections.title: What We Need From You
sections.html:
Send us the county and legal description if you have it, along with any deed, lease, or royalty paperwork on hand. We'll pull the rest from Wyoming county records and come back with a written offer and a straightforward closing process that doesn't require you to leave your home state.

If you're not sure what county your family's minerals are even in, that's a common starting point too. Old family paperwork, even incomplete, is usually enough for us to trace it.

sections.title: When the Family Land Feels Like Someone Else's State
sections.html:
For heirs who've never visited Wyoming and have no plans to, a mineral interest here can feel less like an asset and more like an obligation attached to a place they don't otherwise think about. That's a completely understandable position, and it's often the deciding factor for out-of-state owners who choose to sell rather than continue managing something disconnected from the rest of their life.

Other families keep the connection deliberately, treating a small Wyoming royalty check as a tie to where a grandparent or great-grandparent once lived and worked. Either choice is reasonable. We just make sure the distance itself never becomes the reason a fair deal doesn't happen.

faqs.q: Do you have to travel to Wyoming to sell your mineral rights?
faqs.a: No. We handle the entire process remotely by mail, phone, and email, including notarized closing documents sent wherever you live.

faqs.q: You have lost track of which county your family's minerals are in. Can you help?
faqs.a: Yes. Send whatever old paperwork or family information you have, and we can often trace the property through Wyoming county records.

faqs.q: Is it harder to sell an out-of-state interest than one owned locally?
faqs.a: Not for us. Location of the owner doesn't affect what your minerals are worth. We evaluate the property itself, wherever you happen to live.

faqs.q: How do closing documents work if you are not in Wyoming?
faqs.a: Documents can be notarized at your local bank, UPS store, or notary service and returned to us by mail. We coordinate the timing so nothing gets held up.

faqs.q: Should you update your mailing address with the operator even if you plan to sell?
faqs.a: It doesn't hurt, but if you're selling, the buyer will handle updating ownership records going forward, so it's not essential before a sale closes.

items.name: Minerals in Probate & Estates
items.meta: Settling an estate with Wyoming mineral rights in it? We work with executors and personal representatives to value and buy interests during probate.

sections.html:
An executor closing out an estate that includes mineral rights has one more asset to account for, and it's usually the one nobody in the family fully understands.

Wyoming estates with oil and gas interests come across our desk from executors and personal representatives regularly, often as one line item among several the estate has to resolve — a house, a vehicle, some savings, and a mineral interest nobody quite knows the value of. The court, the beneficiaries, or both need a real number, and the executor needs it fast enough not to hold up the rest of the estate.

We work directly with executors and estate attorneys to get that number, and to close a sale if the estate decides selling makes sense, all within the timeline the probate court has set.

sections.title: The Executor's Job With a Mineral Asset
sections.html:
An executor has a duty to account for estate assets accurately, and that includes mineral interests even when they're small, non-producing, or confusing to value. Wyoming probate typically requires an inventory listing estate property, and a mineral interest needs a defensible valuation on that inventory just like any other asset.

We can provide a written valuation for inventory purposes whether or not the estate ultimately decides to sell. If the beneficiaries later choose to sell as part of settling the estate or distributing proceeds, that same relationship carries forward into an actual purchase offer.

sections.title: Selling During Probate vs. After Distribution
sections.html:
Depending on the estate's structure and Wyoming probate rules, a sale of mineral rights may happen while the estate is still open, with the executor signing on the estate's behalf, or after the interest has been distributed to beneficiaries who then decide individually whether to sell. Which path applies depends on the will's terms, whether the estate needs liquidity to pay debts or taxes, and what the probate court has authorized.

We can work either way. If the estate needs to sell during probate to raise cash for expenses, we move at the pace the court process allows. If the minerals will be distributed first and beneficiaries decide afterward, we're ready for that conversation too, whenever it happens.

sections.title: Multiple Beneficiaries, One Interest
sections.html:
It's common for a mineral interest to be left to several beneficiaries jointly rather than one heir. After distribution, that can mean multiple family members each holding a fractional share, deciding independently whether to sell. We handle that the same way we handle any multi-owner situation — buying from whichever heirs want to sell, without requiring unanimous agreement.

If the will or the estate plan calls for the interest to be sold and proceeds split among beneficiaries, we can also work directly with the executor to make one clean transaction rather than several separate ones.

sections.title: Getting Started
sections.html:
Send us the deed or legal description for the mineral interest, the county where it's located, and any production or lease history you have. If you're the executor, let us know where the estate stands in the probate process so we can move at the right pace for your situation.

This isn't legal or tax advice about how to administer the estate — talk to your attorney or CPA about those decisions. What we provide is a real, documented valuation and, if the estate chooses, a straightforward purchase.

sections.title: Small Estates and Simplified Procedures
sections.html:
Wyoming has simplified procedures for smaller estates that can sometimes avoid a full probate process, and mineral interests with modest value may qualify depending on the estate's total size and the specific county's practices. Whether your estate qualifies is a question for the estate's attorney, not us, but it's worth asking early, since a simplified process can move considerably faster than full probate.

Even under a simplified procedure, the mineral interest still needs an honest valuation to satisfy whatever documentation the county or the beneficiaries require. We provide that valuation the same way regardless of which probate path the estate takes.

faqs.q: Can you provide a valuation for probate inventory purposes even before the estate is ready to sell?
faqs.a: Yes. We can provide a written valuation to help satisfy inventory requirements, with no obligation to sell.

faqs.q: Do you work directly with estate attorneys?
faqs.a: Yes, we coordinate directly with attorneys and executors to make sure paperwork and timing line up with the probate process.

faqs.q: Can the estate sell minerals before they're distributed to beneficiaries?
faqs.a: Often, depending on the will's terms and what the probate court authorizes, particularly if the estate needs liquidity. Your attorney can confirm what applies to your case.

faqs.q: What if multiple beneficiaries inherit the same interest and disagree on selling?
faqs.a: Each beneficiary can typically decide independently about their own share once distributed. We can buy from those who want to sell without requiring everyone to agree.

faqs.q: Does the estate owe taxes on a mineral rights sale?
faqs.a: Possibly, depending on the estate's basis and value at death. The executor should consult the estate's CPA or tax advisor about the specific tax treatment.

items.name: Fractional & Small Interests
items.meta: Own a sixteenth, a thirty-second, or smaller? We buy small fractional mineral interests across Wyoming, no matter how many heirs are on the deed.

sections.html:
A quarter section split four generations deep can leave you owning a sixty-fourth of the minerals under it. That's still a real, saleable interest, and we buy interests that size regularly.

Every generation a mineral estate passes through without being sold divides it a little further. A grandparent's undivided half interest becomes four grandchildren's eighths, then their children's sixteenths, and by the third or fourth generation a family can have a dozen relatives each holding a fraction too small to matter much individually, but adding up to real acreage collectively.

Buyers who insist on a minimum interest size, or who won't deal with more than one or two owners on a tract, leave a lot of Wyoming families stuck holding a small piece of paper that never produces cash and never gets resolved. We don't work that way — small fractional interests are a normal part of our business, not an exception.

sections.title: Why Interests Keep Getting Smaller
sections.html:
Original homestead and railroad-era mineral reservations in Wyoming were often held by a single family or a small handful of original patent holders. A century of intestate succession, wills that split minerals equally among children, and second and third marriages layering in more heirs has fractionalized a lot of that original acreage many times over. It's the same pattern that plays out in county clerk records across the state, section after section.

The result is that a single producing tract can have twenty or thirty names on the division order, each getting a royalty check for a few dollars a month that barely covers the cost of the stamp to mail it. Consolidating those small pieces into fewer hands, through purchase, is often the only practical way any of it gets managed efficiently again.

sections.title: Small Doesn't Mean Worthless
sections.html:
A sixty-fourth interest in a producing unit under an active Powder River or Green River well is still worth pricing honestly, based on the same production data, decline curve, and net mineral acreage math we'd use on a full interest. The dollar figure is smaller because the fraction is smaller, not because the underlying minerals are less real.

Where fractional interests get complicated is when heirs disagree about whether to sell, or when some heirs can't be located. We buy from individual co-owners on their own fractional share even if other family members choose to keep theirs, so one relative wanting to sell doesn't have to wait on the whole family to agree.

sections.title: Cleaning Up the Paper Trail
sections.html:
Fractional interests often come with title complications that a single-owner tract doesn't have — unprobated estates two generations back, a name misspelled on one deed in the chain, an heir who moved out of state and stopped responding to mail decades ago. County clerk and recorder records can usually sort this out, but it takes someone willing to actually pull and read the chain of title, deed by deed.

We do that work as part of every fractional purchase. If your chain of title has a gap, that doesn't automatically stop a sale, but it does affect the paperwork needed to close, and we'll walk you through exactly what's required before you sign anything.

sections.title: What to Send Us
sections.html:
The most useful starting point is whatever you already have — a division order, a royalty check stub, an old deed, or even just the county and a rough legal description if that's all that survived. From there we can pull the rest of the record ourselves.

If you know your interest is small, don't assume that means it's not worth the trouble of selling. A lot of families are surprised the fraction adds up to a real number once we walk through the math with them.

sections.title: Consolidation Benefits the Whole Family
sections.html:
When one heir sells their fractional share, it doesn't just simplify that person's finances. It also means one fewer name on the division order for the operator to track, one fewer set of mailing address updates to chase, and one fewer signature needed the next time the family wants to negotiate a new lease together. Consolidation, even piece by piece, tends to make the remaining ownership easier to manage for everyone still holding a share.

We've bought individual fractional interests out of families where a dozen relatives were on the same tract, and over a few years watched the ownership consolidate down to just a handful of names as different heirs decided selling made sense for their own situation. There's no requirement that the whole family move at the same pace.

faqs.q: Is there a minimum size interest you'll buy?
faqs.a: No. We regularly buy interests as small as a sixty-fourth or smaller. The offer reflects the fraction and underlying acreage honestly, not a minimum threshold.

faqs.q: Do all the heirs have to agree to sell?
faqs.a: No. We can purchase an individual co-owner's fractional share directly, without requiring every other heir on the deed to participate.

faqs.q: What if the family does not know exactly what fraction it owns?
faqs.a: That's common with old fractionalized interests. We pull the deed chain from county records to calculate your exact fraction as part of preparing an offer.

faqs.q: One of the heirs on the family's minerals can't be found. Does that stop a sale?
faqs.a: It doesn't stop the heirs who can be located from selling their own share. We can talk through options for the rest depending on your title situation.

faqs.q: Is it worth selling a tiny interest instead of just keeping it?
faqs.a: That depends on your goals, but many owners prefer a real payment now over years of small, irregular checks and the paperwork of tracking an interest that costs more to manage than it earns.

items.name: Leased but Undrilled
items.meta: Collected a lease bonus but no well has been drilled yet? We buy Wyoming mineral rights under an active lease, producing or not.

sections.html:
You signed a lease, cashed the bonus check, and then nothing happened. That's not unusual, and it doesn't mean your minerals aren't worth selling right now.

A lot of Wyoming mineral owners are sitting on acreage under an active oil and gas lease with no rig in sight. The company paid a bonus per acre to hold the lease, the primary term is ticking down, and there's been no permit, no rig, no announcement. That gap between signing and drilling can run a few years or longer depending on the operator's plans and the basin's pace of development.

We buy interests in exactly this position all the time. An active lease with an unmet drilling obligation is a real, valuable asset, not a dead end, and we price it based on what it actually represents rather than treating the lack of a well as a reason to lowball you.

sections.title: What an Active Lease Actually Means for Value
sections.html:
A signed lease tells us a company was interested enough in your acreage to pay a bonus for the right to drill it, which is itself information about how the area is regarded. It also sets the royalty rate you'd receive if a well does go in, and that rate transfers to a buyer along with the minerals, so it's a fixed term worth accounting for in the price.

What we look at closely is the primary term remaining, whether the lease has any extension or delay rental provisions, and what's happening on nearby acreage. A lease with two years left in an area seeing active permitting nearby is worth more than one with six months left and no nearby activity, even though both are technically leased and undrilled.

sections.title: Why Operators Sit on Leases
sections.html:
Companies lease more acreage than they can drill in a given year for a lot of ordinary business reasons — building a large enough contiguous block for efficient horizontal spacing, sequencing development across a multi-year program, or simply prioritizing their strongest acreage first and holding the rest. None of that is a comment on the quality of your specific minerals.

It does mean the timeline to actual production is uncertain, and uncertainty is exactly what a lot of owners would rather not sit with, especially if the lease is getting close to its primary term and could either extend, expire, or finally see a permit filed.

sections.title: What Happens If the Lease Expires Unproduced
sections.html:
If a lease reaches the end of its primary term without a well drilled and without an extension, it typically terminates and the minerals revert to you unencumbered, free to be leased again to a new operator or sold outright. That's not necessarily bad for you as an owner, but it does restart the clock on when you'd see any bonus or royalty income.

Selling before that expiration locks in value now rather than betting on either a new lease bonus or a future well that may or may not get drilled. Selling after expiration is also an option, and we price unleased, undrilled acreage too, just on a different basis tied more heavily to area activity than to a specific lease's terms.

sections.title: Getting an Offer on a Leased Interest
sections.html:
Send us a copy of the lease along with your deed or legal description. We'll check the county record to confirm the lease is properly filed, look at the remaining term and royalty rate, and review nearby permitting and drilling activity before putting a number together.

You don't need the lease to expire, or a well to get drilled, before you can sell. The lease itself, and what it says about your acreage, is part of what we're pricing.

sections.title: Reading Your Lease Before You Decide
sections.html:
Every lease is a little different, and the details matter more than owners usually expect. Some leases include a shut-in royalty clause that keeps the lease alive even without production. Others have Pugh clauses that release undeveloped portions of a larger tract after the primary term. A lease with a continuous drilling obligation behaves differently from one that doesn't. We read through your specific lease language as part of preparing an offer, not only the bonus amount and the term dates.

If you're not sure what any of those terms mean for your situation, that's normal. Most owners aren't lease attorneys, and we're glad to walk through what your specific lease says in plain language before you decide anything.

faqs.q: Can you sell your minerals while they're still under an active lease?
faqs.a: Yes. The lease transfers with the sale, so the buyer steps into your position as lessor, still entitled to royalties if a well is drilled during the lease term.

faqs.q: Does selling change your lease terms?
faqs.a: No. The existing lease's royalty rate and terms stay in place; ownership of the underlying minerals and the right to future royalty payments transfers to the buyer.

faqs.q: What if the lease expires before a well is ever drilled?
faqs.a: The lease typically terminates and the minerals revert to you unencumbered. You could then lease again to a new operator or sell the interest outright.

faqs.q: Is a leased-but-undrilled interest worth less than a producing one?
faqs.a: Usually, since there's no current royalty stream, but it still carries real value tied to the lease terms, remaining term, and nearby drilling activity. We price it on those factors rather than treating it as worthless.

faqs.q: How do you know how much time is left on your lease?
faqs.a: Your lease document states the primary term and its start date. If you don't have a copy, we can often locate the recorded lease through the county clerk's office.

image.alt: Leased but Undrilled mineral rights

items.name: Non-Producing Minerals
items.meta: No wells, no lease, no royalty checks. Non-producing Wyoming mineral acreage still has value tied to nearby activity. Get a written offer from us.

sections.html:
No royalty checks, no lease, maybe no activity you've ever heard about on the tract at all. Non-producing doesn't mean worthless, and we buy this kind of acreage every week.

Plenty of mineral owners in Wyoming hold acreage that's never seen a drill bit. Maybe it's in a county with scattered activity rather than a dense field. Maybe it sits on the flank of a play where the core got drilled but the edges haven't. Maybe a lease from years ago expired without a well and nobody's re-leased it since. Whatever the reason, no current income doesn't mean no current value.

We price non-producing minerals on a different basis than producing ones, and we're upfront that it's a different number. But it's not a nominal number just because there's no royalty check to point to. Real activity nearby, formation potential under your specific tract, and lease bonus trends in the area all feed into what we offer.

sections.title: How We Value Acreage With No Production History
sections.html:
Without a decline curve or royalty statement to work from, we lean on comparable data instead: recent lease bonuses paid on nearby tracts, permitting and spacing activity in your section and the surrounding ones, and which formations are known to be productive in your specific area of the basin. Wyoming counties keep detailed records of filed leases and permits, and that record is where a real number starts.

Proximity matters a lot here. A non-producing tract two sections away from an active horizontal drilling program is worth meaningfully more than one in an area that's seen no activity in a decade, even though neither one has a current royalty check. We check exactly where your acreage sits relative to what's currently being drilled before we make an offer.

sections.title: Expired Leases Are Common, Not a Red Flag
sections.html:
A lot of non-producing acreage carries a history of one or more expired leases — a company held it for a few years during an earlier phase of basin interest, paid a bonus, never drilled, and let the lease lapse. That's a completely normal pattern and doesn't indicate anything wrong with the minerals themselves. Companies let leases expire for their own portfolio reasons all the time, not because of anything specific to your tract.

If your acreage has an expired lease history, that record actually helps us, because it shows what a real operator was once willing to pay for the right to drill it, even if they ultimately moved on to other priorities.

sections.title: Selling Now vs. Waiting for a Lease
sections.html:
Some owners hold non-producing minerals hoping a company eventually offers a new lease bonus. That can happen, but there's no set timeline, and it depends entirely on whether operators expand development toward your specific section. Selling now converts an uncertain future possibility into a certain payment today.

Other owners are comfortable waiting, and that's a reasonable choice too, especially if there's specific reason to think activity is heading their direction. We're not going to tell you waiting is always wrong. We'll tell you honestly what we see happening nearby so you can decide with real information.

sections.title: What We Need to Evaluate Your Tract
sections.html:
A legal description and the county your minerals sit in is the minimum we need to start. If you have any old lease paperwork, even expired, send that too, since it tells us about the tract's history even if it's no longer active.

From there we check county records, permitting activity, and nearby drilling trends before coming back with a written offer that reflects what your specific acreage looks like today, not a generic basin-wide guess.

sections.title: Formation Potential Under Your Specific Tract
sections.html:
Not every acre in a basin sits over the same rock. Two neighboring sections can have different formation thickness, different depth to the pay zone, or sit on opposite sides of a fault that changes how a horizontal well would be landed. We look at publicly available well log and permitting data near your tract, where it exists, to understand what formations are realistically in play under your specific acreage rather than assuming the whole county is uniform.

This is part of why two owners with the same acreage count in different sections of the same county can get meaningfully different offers from us. We're pricing your ground, not a basin-wide average.

faqs.q: If your minerals have never produced, do they have any real value?
faqs.a: Often yes, tied to nearby drilling activity, formation potential, and lease bonus trends in your area, even without a royalty history. We evaluate it on that basis rather than treating it as worthless.

faqs.q: Your lease expired years ago with no well drilled. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: No, it's common and doesn't reflect poorly on your minerals. It actually shows an operator once valued the acreage enough to pay a bonus for it.

faqs.q: Should you wait for a new lease offer instead of selling?
faqs.a: That depends on whether activity is trending toward your area. We can tell you what we see happening nearby so you can weigh waiting against selling now with real information.

faqs.q: What documents do you need if there's no current lease or production?
faqs.a: A legal description and county are the minimum. Any old deed or expired lease paperwork you have helps but isn't required to get a starting offer.

faqs.q: How is the offer calculated without a royalty check to base it on?
faqs.a: We use recent lease bonus activity, permitting trends, and formation data for your specific section and surrounding area, drawn from county and state records.

items.name: Trust-Owned Minerals
items.meta: Serving as trustee over Wyoming mineral rights? We work with trustees to value and purchase trust-owned interests within the trust's authority.

sections.html:
A trustee managing mineral rights held in trust has obligations to the beneficiaries that a private owner doesn't, and that changes how a sale needs to be handled from the first phone call.

Mineral rights placed into a trust, whether for estate planning, asset protection, or ongoing family management, come with a trustee who has a fiduciary duty to manage them prudently. That duty applies whether the trustee decides to hold the interest, lease it, or sell it, and it means documentation matters more here than in a straightforward individual sale.

We work with trustees across Wyoming regularly, and we understand the trust needs a defensible, documented transaction, not a handshake and a check alone. That's how we operate with every seller, but for a trustee it's not optional.

sections.title: The Trustee's Fiduciary Duty
sections.html:
A trustee is required to act in the best interest of the trust's beneficiaries, which generally means getting fair value for any asset sold and documenting the basis for that decision. Selling a mineral interest without a real, written valuation exposes the trustee to questions later from beneficiaries who might wonder whether the price was fair.

We provide a written offer with the reasoning behind it — production history where it exists, comparable lease and sale activity in the area, and formation and basin context — so the trustee has something concrete to point to if the decision is ever reviewed.

sections.title: What the Trust Document Allows
sections.html:
Before anything else, the trust instrument itself typically governs whether the trustee has authority to sell mineral interests outright, and whether that authority requires beneficiary consent, court approval, or neither. Some trusts give a trustee broad discretion over asset management; others are more restrictive, especially around real property and mineral interests specifically.

We're not able to interpret your trust document for you — that's a question for the attorney who drafted it or who currently advises the trust. Once you know what authority you have, we can move forward with valuation and, if appropriate, purchase.

sections.title: Documentation We Provide
sections.html:
For a trust sale, we typically provide a more detailed written offer than we would for an informal individual transaction, specifically because a trustee needs to show their work. That includes the basis for the valuation, the county and legal description confirmed against the title record, and clear closing documentation naming the trust as seller.

If the trust requires co-trustee signatures, beneficiary notice, or any other internal procedural step before a sale, let us know early so we can build that into the closing timeline rather than discovering it at the last minute.

sections.title: Multiple Trusts, Multiple Generations
sections.html:
It's not unusual to find mineral interests split across several family trusts after estate planning restructured ownership over multiple generations, sometimes alongside interests still held individually by family members outside any trust. We can work with trustees on each trust's portion separately, or coordinate a single closing across multiple trusts and individual owners if that's simpler for the family.

Whatever the structure, the process starts the same way: confirm what the trust actually owns through county records, confirm the trustee's authority to sell, and then put together a documented offer.

sections.title: Successor Trustees and Changed Circumstances
sections.html:
Trusts sometimes change hands between trustees over the years, and a successor trustee stepping in may inherit mineral interests they know little about, along with whatever records the prior trustee kept, which can range from thorough to nearly nonexistent. If you're a successor trustee trying to get a handle on trust-owned minerals for the first time, we can help reconstruct the ownership picture from county records rather than relying solely on whatever files were handed off.

This comes up more often than you'd expect, especially with trusts that have held Wyoming minerals for decades without much active management. Getting current, documented information is usually the first useful step before deciding whether to hold, lease, or sell.

faqs.q: Does the trustee need beneficiary approval to sell mineral rights?
faqs.a: It depends on the specific trust document. Some trusts give the trustee broad discretion; others require consent or notice. Review your trust instrument with the trust's attorney to confirm.

faqs.q: Can you provide documentation to support the sale price for the trust's records?
faqs.a: Yes. We provide a written offer with the valuation basis included, which trustees typically keep as part of the trust's records to support the decision.

faqs.q: What if the mineral interest is split across multiple family trusts?
faqs.a: We can work with each trustee separately or coordinate a combined closing, depending on what works best for the family and the trusts involved.

faqs.q: Do you need a copy of the trust document?
faqs.a: Often yes, or at least the relevant sections confirming trustee authority and the trust's name as titled owner, so the closing documents match the trust's legal structure correctly.

faqs.q: Is selling trust-owned minerals different from an individual sale in terms of timeline?
faqs.a: It can take somewhat longer if internal trust procedures, like co-trustee signatures, need to be completed, but the underlying valuation and title work is the same process.

items.name: Selling for Liquidity
items.meta: Need cash for medical bills, retirement, or debt? Selling your Wyoming mineral rights converts a slow royalty trickle into one lump-sum payment now.

sections.html:
A royalty check that trickles in a few hundred dollars at a time doesn't help much when the bill in front of you is a real number due this month. Selling converts that trickle into one payment.

There are a handful of reasons Wyoming mineral owners come to us needing cash rather than continued royalty income: a medical bill that can't wait for eighteen months of checks to add up, retirement income that needs to be more predictable than an oil price swing allows, a debt that's accruing interest faster than royalties are paying it down, or just wanting to simplify finances at a point in life where fewer moving pieces is worth more than a small monthly check.

Whatever the reason, the math is usually the same. A mineral interest paying modest royalties over many years represents a certain lump-sum value today, discounted for time and risk. If your need for cash is now, waiting for those payments to arrive one small check at a time often costs you more in stress and missed opportunity than the wait is worth.

sections.title: When a Lump Sum Beats a Trickle
sections.html:
Royalty checks are, by nature, unpredictable in size and timing. Commodity prices swing, wells decline, operators sometimes fall behind on payment schedules. If you're counting on that income to cover something specific and time-sensitive, the uncertainty itself is a cost, separate from the total dollar amount you'd eventually collect.

Converting the interest to a lump sum removes that uncertainty. You know exactly what you're getting and when, which matters a lot more when you're facing a medical bill, a debt with a due date, or a retirement budget that needs to be reliable rather than hopeful.

sections.title: Medical and Emergency Expenses
sections.html:
Medical debt doesn't wait for a well to keep producing at a steady rate. We've worked with owners who needed funds fast for a procedure, a family member's care, or an unexpected emergency, and a mineral sale closed in weeks did more for them than years of royalty checks would have on the same timeline.

We move as fast as the county title work allows, and we're upfront if something in your specific chain of title is going to slow things down, so you're not caught off guard by a closing date that doesn't match your need.

sections.title: Retirement and Fixed-Income Planning
sections.html:
Royalty income is a poor substitute for a stable retirement budget precisely because it isn't stable — it moves with commodity prices and well decline in ways a fixed pension or annuity doesn't. Some retirees prefer to convert a mineral interest into cash that can be placed into something more predictable, or simply used directly, rather than budgeting around a royalty check that might be different every quarter.

This is a financial planning decision, and we'd rather you make it with your financial advisor's input than ours alone. We can tell you what the interest is worth today; your advisor can tell you how that fits your broader retirement picture.

sections.title: Debt and Simplification
sections.html:
Paying down high-interest debt with a lump sum from a mineral sale often makes more financial sense than letting royalty income arrive slowly while interest keeps compounding on the debt side. We've seen owners do exactly this math and come out ahead by selling rather than waiting.

Others simply want fewer financial accounts and mailing addresses to track as they get older, and a small royalty interest that generates a modest, irregular check is often the first thing to go when someone's simplifying their affairs.

sections.title: Comparing the Real Numbers
sections.html:
Before deciding whether a lump sum or continued royalty income makes more sense for your situation, it helps to look at actual figures rather than a general feeling. What has the interest paid over the last two or three years? What's the trend — flat, declining, or growing? What would the total look like if that trend continued for another five or ten years, discounted for the risk that it doesn't hold steady?

We can walk through that comparison with you using your real royalty statements alongside our offer, so the decision is based on your specific numbers rather than a general assumption about which option is usually better.

faqs.q: How fast can a mineral rights sale close if you need cash quickly?
faqs.a: It depends on the county title work involved, but a clean chain of title can often close in a few weeks. We'll tell you upfront if anything in your specific case will take longer.

faqs.q: Is selling mineral rights better than taking out a loan against them?
faqs.a: It depends on your situation and the loan terms available to you. A sale avoids ongoing interest and debt, while a loan keeps ownership. Talk through the numbers with your financial advisor.

faqs.q: Will you owe taxes on the sale proceeds?
faqs.a: Possibly, depending on your basis in the minerals and the sale price. Consult your CPA or tax advisor about your specific situation before finalizing a sale.

faqs.q: Can you sell just part of your interest instead of all of it?
faqs.a: Often yes, depending on the interest and how it's held. We can discuss whether a partial sale makes sense if you want to keep some royalty income while raising cash now.

faqs.q: Is a lump sum always worth more than waiting for royalty checks?
faqs.a: Not always in raw total dollars over a very long horizon, but for owners who need funds now or want predictability, the certainty of a lump sum often outweighs an uncertain, slower royalty stream.

items.name: Mineral Rights in Divorce
items.meta: Mineral rights are marital property that has to be divided or valued in a Wyoming divorce. We buy interests outright so a settlement can close clean.

sections.html:
A mineral interest acquired or inherited during a marriage almost always has to be addressed in the settlement, and half of a royalty stream is a lot harder to split fairly than a bank account.

Wyoming courts divide marital property equitably, and mineral rights count, whether they came from a family inheritance, a purchase, or a lease bonus paid during the marriage. Two people who used to be one household now need two clean outcomes, and a mineral interest doesn't split down the middle the way cash does.

We see three patterns most often in a divorce: one spouse buys out the other's share of the interest, the couple sells the whole interest and splits the proceeds, or the settlement assigns the minerals to one party and the other walks away with a different asset of comparable value. All three need a real number on the table before an attorney can draft the decree, and that's usually where we come in.

sections.title: Why a Royalty Stream Is Hard to Split in a Decree
sections.html:
A house can be appraised and sold or refinanced. A mineral interest with an active royalty check is harder, because its value depends on decline curve, remaining reserves, and commodity price, not simply a comparable sale down the street. Courts and attorneys need a defensible number, not a guess, and that number has to hold up if either party questions it later.

If the interest isn't producing at all, that's its own complication, because there's no check history to point to and the value sits entirely in future potential. We price both producing and non-producing interests the same way we'd price them for any seller, which gives your attorney a real figure to work with instead of a placeholder.

sections.title: One Spouse Keeping the Minerals, One Cashing Out
sections.html:
A common resolution is for one spouse to keep the mineral interest and the other to receive cash or another asset equal to their share. We can provide a written offer on the full interest so both sides and their attorneys have a real market number to negotiate the buyout against, rather than an informal estimate from a relative who used to work in the oilfield.

If the spouse keeping the minerals later decides they'd rather have the cash than manage a royalty interest going forward, that offer stays available. A lot of people take on minerals in a settlement because it felt easier than fighting over the number, then sell within a year or two once the divorce is settled and they want a clean break from the paperwork.

sections.title: Both Parties Ready to Sell and Split
sections.html:
When neither spouse wants to hold onto the interest, selling outright and splitting the proceeds according to the settlement terms is often the simplest path. We can close with both parties on the deed, or after the decree assigns the interest to one party who then sells individually, whichever order your attorney recommends for your county and case.

Either way, we need the legal description of the property, the county where the minerals sit, and whatever paperwork exists — deed, lease, or royalty statement — to put a number together. We'll work directly with your attorney if that's easier for your timeline.

sections.title: Timing With the Settlement
sections.html:
Divorce settlements often run on a court-imposed schedule, and mineral title work can take longer than either party expects if there's a fractional interest, an old lease, or a title issue from a prior generation. We start the county records review as soon as you send us the legal description, so the offer and the closing timeline can move alongside your attorney's deadlines instead of holding them up.

We're not your attorney and don't give legal advice about the divorce itself. What we do is put a fair, documented number on the mineral asset so the people who are handling the legal side have something solid to negotiate with.

faqs.q: Do mineral rights count as marital property in Wyoming?
faqs.a: Generally yes, if acquired or inherited during the marriage, though the specific facts of your case matter. Talk to your attorney about how your minerals are classified in your settlement.

faqs.q: Can you value a mineral interest that isn't producing yet?
faqs.a: Yes. We price non-producing acreage based on nearby drilling activity, lease bonus trends, and formation potential, the same way we'd approach it for any seller.

faqs.q: Will you work directly with the attorneys?
faqs.a: Yes, we regularly coordinate with attorneys on both sides to make sure the offer and closing paperwork line up with the settlement terms and timeline.

faqs.q: What if only one of us wants to sell?
faqs.a: We can make an offer on the full interest so both parties have a real number to negotiate a buyout against, even if only one spouse ultimately signs to sell.

faqs.q: How fast can this close before the court date?
faqs.a: It depends on the county title work and whether there are fractional or legacy ownership issues. Send us the legal description early so we can start the records review right away.
