interest-types.title: Mineral Interest Types

items.name: Mineral Rights
items.meta: Own the minerals under Wyoming land, separate from the surface? We buy full mineral interests statewide, producing or not.

sections.html:
Owning the minerals under a piece of Wyoming ground is a different thing than owning the ground itself, and a lot of owners hold one without the other. If your deed says minerals, we can put a number on it.

A mineral interest is the ownership of everything below the surface — oil, gas, coal, and other substances — separate and apart from ownership of the surface land itself. Wyoming has a long history of severing these two estates, going back to homestead-era reservations, railroad land grants, and coal company transactions from a century ago, so it's common for the person who owns the surface today to have no connection at all to who owns the minerals underneath it.

If you hold a mineral interest, you own the right to explore for and produce oil and gas from that tract, or to lease that right to an operator in exchange for a bonus payment and ongoing royalty. That's the full bundle of rights, and it's the most complete, most valuable form of ownership in the oil and gas business, more so than a royalty-only or overriding interest carved out of it.

sections.title: What a Full Mineral Interest Actually Includes
sections.html:
Owning the minerals outright means you control whether the tract gets leased at all, who it gets leased to, and on what terms — royalty rate, bonus per acre, primary term length. Once leased, you receive royalty payments on production, typically without bearing any of the drilling or operating costs, since those fall on the operator under the lease.

This is different from owning just a royalty interest, which is a right to payment without the leasing control, or a working interest, which carries drilling costs alongside the upside. A full mineral owner sits in the strongest negotiating position of the three, because everything downstream — the lease terms, the royalty rate, whether a well gets drilled at all — starts with a decision only the mineral owner can make.

sections.title: How Wyoming Deeds Reserve or Convey Minerals
sections.html:
Mineral ownership in Wyoming traces back through deed language that either conveys the minerals along with the surface, reserves them for the grantor while selling the surface, or severs them entirely into a standalone mineral deed. County clerk and recorder records show this chain, tract by tract, and reading it correctly is the difference between knowing what you actually own versus assuming based on a family story.

It's common to find a deed from the 1940s or 1950s that reserved minerals when a ranch sold its surface, with the mineral interest then passing down through the reserving family's estate ever since, sometimes fractionalizing along the way, while the surface changed hands to entirely unrelated owners multiple times. Neither owner has any claim on the other's estate, and that separation is permanent unless both parties agree otherwise.

sections.title: The Wyoming Checkerboard and Federal Minerals
sections.html:
Across a wide swath of southern Wyoming, federal mineral ownership checkerboards with private mineral ownership in an alternating pattern of sections, a legacy of the 1862 Pacific Railway Act land grants to the Union Pacific Railroad. Odd-numbered sections in that corridor were typically granted to the railroad and eventually passed into private hands; even-numbered sections stayed federal, administered by the BLM.

If your minerals sit in that corridor, knowing whether your specific section is private or federal changes the entire transaction — federal minerals carry BLM-set royalty terms, require federal lease assignment paperwork, and move through a different, generally slower process than a straight private deed. We check this against county plat records before we ever quote a number, so you know upfront which kind of asset you're actually holding.

sections.title: Getting Your Interest Valued
sections.html:
Whether your mineral interest is producing, leased but undrilled, or sitting undeveloped, we price it based on real factors: current production and decline curve where it exists, nearby drilling and permitting activity, lease bonus trends in your specific area, and the formation your tract sits over. We don't use a flat statewide number, because a mineral interest in the Powder River Basin and one in the Green River Basin are priced on completely different data.

Send us your legal description, county, and whatever deed or production paperwork you have, and we'll pull the rest from the courthouse record ourselves before coming back with a written offer.

faqs.q: What's the difference between mineral rights and surface rights?
faqs.a: Mineral rights cover ownership of oil, gas, and other subsurface substances. Surface rights cover ownership of the land itself. Wyoming deeds frequently separate the two, so one person can own the surface while another owns the minerals underneath.

faqs.q: How do you know if you own the minerals under your property?
faqs.a: Check your deed's language, or the deed history in the county clerk and recorder's office where the property sits. Many Wyoming surface owners don't own the minerals below their land, and many mineral owners have never owned or lived on the surface at all.

faqs.q: Do you buy both producing and non-producing mineral interests?
faqs.a: Yes. We price producing interests based on current royalty income and decline trends, and non-producing interests based on nearby activity, formation potential, and lease bonus history.

faqs.q: What is the Wyoming checkerboard and how does it affect your minerals?
faqs.a: It's the alternating pattern of private and federal mineral ownership left over from 19th-century railroad land grants across parts of southern Wyoming. It affects royalty terms and closing paperwork, and we check for it as part of every offer.

faqs.q: Is owning full mineral rights better than owning a royalty interest?
faqs.a: A full mineral interest generally carries more control and value than a royalty-only interest, since it includes the right to negotiate leases and decide whether to lease at all. Both are real, saleable assets.

image.alt: Mineral Rights mineral rights

items.name: Royalty Interests
items.meta: Getting royalty checks from a Wyoming well but don't own the leasing rights? We buy royalty interests statewide. Get a written offer on your stream.

sections.html:
A royalty interest gets you a check when the well produces and no bill when it doesn't. That's the whole deal, and it's a real asset we buy regularly.

A royalty interest is the right to a share of production revenue from a well, free of the costs of drilling and operating it. It's distinct from owning the underlying minerals outright, which includes the right to lease the ground and negotiate terms. Most royalty owners in Wyoming got there one of two ways: they leased their own minerals to an operator and retained a royalty under that lease, or they inherited or purchased a royalty interest that had already been carved out of someone else's mineral ownership.

Whichever path brought you here, a royalty interest pays out as a percentage of the value of oil and gas produced, typically a percentage of gross proceeds before drilling and lease operating costs are deducted, though the exact deduction treatment depends on your specific lease or conveyance language.

sections.title: Landowner Royalty vs. Purchased Royalty
sections.html:
A landowner royalty is what a mineral owner keeps when they sign an oil and gas lease — commonly one-eighth historically, though modern Wyoming leases in active basins often run higher depending on negotiating position and competition among operators at the time of leasing. That royalty stays with the mineral owner as long as the lease is in effect and the well produces.

A purchased or inherited royalty interest, sometimes called a non-participating royalty depending on how it was created, is a standalone asset that doesn't carry the right to negotiate future leases, just the right to a defined percentage of production revenue. Both types are real, valuable, and separately saleable, but they're valued somewhat differently because of what rights come attached.

sections.title: How Royalty Income Actually Behaves
sections.html:
A royalty check tracks the well's production volume and the commodity price at the time of sale, both of which move constantly. A new well typically peaks in its first year or two, then declines, sometimes steeply for tight shale plays and more gradually for tight gas formations like those in the Green River Basin. Your check size will reflect that curve, and a shrinking check doesn't automatically mean something's wrong — it's usually just the ordinary decline pattern playing out.

Commodity price swings hit on top of that volume decline. Two identical months of oil production can produce very different royalty checks depending on where crude or gas prices sat that month. Reading a royalty statement means separating these two effects — is the check smaller because the well is declining, or because prices moved, or both.

sections.title: What We Look at When Pricing a Royalty Interest
sections.html:
We start with your actual payment history if you have it — division orders, check stubs, or 1099 statements from the operator all help establish the real production and price trend on your specific interest. From there we model the remaining decline curve for the well or wells involved and estimate a realistic value for the future income stream, discounted to reflect that a dollar today is worth more than an uncertain dollar five years from now.

If your royalty interest doesn't come with much payment history, or is tied to a well that hasn't started producing yet, we look at comparable wells nearby in the same formation to build a reasonable estimate instead.

sections.title: Selling a Royalty Interest vs. Continuing to Hold It
sections.html:
A royalty interest is genuinely passive — no operating decisions, no cost exposure, just a check when the well produces. For some owners that's exactly the kind of asset worth keeping long term. For others, the unpredictability of the check size, the eventual decline to a trickle, and the administrative burden of tracking operator changes and tax paperwork make selling for a lump sum the more practical choice.

We buy royalty interests of any size, from a single well's worth of production up to a multi-well portfolio spread across several counties. Send us your division order or the legal description and county, and we'll build a written offer based on your interest's actual production history and remaining potential.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a royalty interest and a mineral interest?
faqs.a: A mineral interest includes the right to lease the property and negotiate terms. A royalty interest is the right to a share of production revenue, without leasing control or drilling cost exposure.

faqs.q: Do you have to pay any of the drilling or operating costs on a royalty interest?
faqs.a: No. Royalty interests are free of drilling and operating costs by definition, which is what separates them from a working interest.

faqs.q: Why has your royalty check gotten smaller over time?
faqs.a: Usually a combination of normal well decline and commodity price movement. Most wells produce most heavily in their first year or two and taper off after that, and price swings compound the effect.

faqs.q: Can you buy your royalty interest if you have only had it a short time?
faqs.a: Yes. Even a short payment history gives us useful data, and we can supplement it with comparable well data nearby if needed to build a fair offer.

faqs.q: Is it better to keep collecting royalty checks or sell for a lump sum?
faqs.a: It depends on your goals. A royalty stream is passive but declining and unpredictable; a lump sum is certain today. We can walk through the real numbers so you decide with actual information.

image.alt: Royalty Interests mineral rights

items.name: Non-Participating Royalty (NPRI)
items.meta: Own a Wyoming NPRI with no say in leasing but a right to production revenue? We buy non-participating royalty interests.

sections.html:
An NPRI gets you paid when the well produces, but you don't get a vote when the lease gets signed. That distinction confuses a lot of owners, and it matters for what your interest is worth.

A non-participating royalty interest, or NPRI, is a right to a share of oil and gas production revenue that was carved out of the underlying mineral estate without the executive right to lease attached. Someone — a grandparent, an estate, a previous seller — reserved or conveyed a royalty percentage while keeping or transferring the leasing authority to somebody else entirely.

That split is common in Wyoming, especially from older deeds where a rancher sold land but reserved a royalty interest for themselves, or an estate divided a mineral interest by giving some heirs the executive rights and others a royalty-only share. If your deed or your family's paperwork uses the term non-participating, that structure is exactly what's going on.

sections.title: What You Don't Control With an NPRI
sections.html:
As an NPRI owner, you have no say over whether the tract gets leased, who it gets leased to, what royalty rate the executive mineral owner negotiates for the underlying estate, or how long the lease term runs. Someone else — the party holding the executive rights — makes all of those decisions, and you simply collect your defined royalty percentage once production begins under whatever lease they signed.

This can be frustrating if you disagree with how the executive owner is managing the leasing, but it's the nature of the interest, and Wyoming courts generally hold executive rights holders to a duty of good faith toward NPRI owners rather than a duty to maximize their return specifically. It's worth understanding that limit before assuming you have more control than you do.

sections.title: What You Do Get With an NPRI
sections.html:
In exchange for giving up leasing control, an NPRI owner typically holds a fixed royalty fraction that doesn't get diluted by however the executive owner structures the lease, depending on the specific language in the reservation or conveyance that created your interest. Once a lease is signed and a well produces, your royalty check flows the same way any royalty owner's would — no drilling costs, no operating costs, just a share of production value.

The exact fraction and whether it's calculated against a specific royalty rate or as a fraction of whatever royalty the executive owner negotiates depends entirely on the deed language that created your NPRI. Reading that language correctly is the first step in valuing the interest accurately.

sections.title: Why NPRI Deed Language Matters So Much
sections.html:
Two NPRIs that look similar on the surface can be worth very different amounts depending on whether the reservation specifies a fixed royalty fraction of production or a fraction of whatever royalty the lease happens to carry. A one-sixteenth NPRI fixed against gross production is worth something different than a one-half interest in whatever royalty the executive owner negotiates, especially if that negotiated royalty rate is on the low end.

We read the actual reservation or conveyance language from the county record before pricing an NPRI, rather than assuming a standard structure, because the difference in how these are drafted directly changes what your interest is worth today and what it would be worth under a future lease.

sections.title: Selling an NPRI
sections.html:
An NPRI is a real, separately saleable asset regardless of whether you have any relationship with whoever holds the executive rights on the same tract. You don't need their permission or involvement to sell your royalty-only interest, and a sale doesn't affect their leasing authority going forward.

Send us your deed or reservation document, along with the county and legal description, and we'll read the language, check production and lease history where it applies, and come back with a written offer that reflects exactly what your NPRI entitles you to.

faqs.q: What does non-participating mean in an NPRI?
faqs.a: It means the interest doesn't include executive rights — the authority to lease the property and negotiate terms. The NPRI owner collects a royalty share but doesn't control leasing decisions.

faqs.q: Do you need permission from the executive rights owner to sell your NPRI?
faqs.a: No. Your NPRI is a separate, independently owned asset. You can sell it without involving or notifying whoever holds the executive rights on the same tract.

faqs.q: Why does your NPRI reservation language matter so much for value?
faqs.a: It determines whether your royalty is a fixed fraction of production or a fraction of whatever royalty rate gets negotiated in a future lease, which can produce very different payouts. We read the actual language before pricing it.

faqs.q: Can you force a lease if the executive owner won't sign one?
faqs.a: Generally no. Wyoming law holds executive owners to a duty of good faith toward NPRI holders, but the decision to lease and its terms remain with the executive rights holder.

faqs.q: Is an NPRI worth less than owning full mineral rights?
faqs.a: Usually, since it lacks leasing control, but it's still a real income-producing or potential asset that we price based on its specific terms and any production history.

items.name: Surface vs. Mineral Estate
items.meta: Confused whether you own the surface, the minerals, or both under your Wyoming land? We explain the split estate and buy mineral interests statewide.

sections.html:
Owning a ranch in Wyoming doesn't automatically mean you own what's under it, and owning minerals here doesn't require ever setting foot on the surface above them.

Wyoming recognizes what's called a split estate, where surface ownership and mineral ownership are treated as two separate, independently transferable pieces of property. A deed can convey the surface and reserve the minerals, convey the minerals and reserve the surface, or convey both together, and once split, the two estates can trade hands entirely independently of each other going forward.

This isn't unusual or a defect in the title. It's a normal, deliberate feature of how Wyoming land has changed hands for over a century, particularly through homestead patents that reserved minerals to the federal government, railroad land grants, and ranch sales that carved out mineral reservations for the selling family.

sections.title: The Dominant Estate Doctrine
sections.html:
Under Wyoming law, the mineral estate is generally considered dominant over the surface estate, meaning the mineral owner or their lessee has the right to use as much of the surface as is reasonably necessary to explore for and produce the minerals, even without the surface owner's consent. That right isn't unlimited — operators must use due regard for the surface owner's use of the land and, for oil and gas specifically, Wyoming's split estate statute requires notice and, in many cases, a surface use agreement or bond before entry.

This dynamic matters differently depending on which side of the split you're on. A surface owner with no mineral rights can find a well pad, road, or pipeline placed on their property without their say in whether it happens, only in how it's done and what compensation applies. A mineral owner benefits from that same dominant right when their own minerals are the ones being developed.

sections.title: Federal Minerals and Wyoming's Checkerboard
sections.html:
A large share of Wyoming's split estate involves federal mineral ownership underlying private surface, a pattern that runs especially deep through the checkerboard corridor across southern Wyoming created by the 1862 Pacific Railway Act grants to the Union Pacific Railroad. Odd-numbered sections went to the railroad and largely became private land over time; even-numbered sections stayed federal. Surface ownership in that corridor followed a similarly mixed pattern, so it's entirely possible to own private surface sitting over federal minerals, or the reverse.

Where minerals are federal, development runs through the Bureau of Land Management's leasing and permitting process rather than a private lease negotiation, and the surface owner's rights and compensation follow a somewhat different framework than they would under a purely private split estate. Knowing which pattern applies to your specific section is something we check against county and, where relevant, BLM records.

sections.title: What This Means If You're Selling Minerals
sections.html:
If you own minerals without the surface, selling your mineral interest doesn't require any involvement from whoever owns the surface today, and it doesn't affect their surface ownership at all. The two estates stay legally separate through the transaction, exactly as they were before it.

If you happen to own both the surface and the minerals together on a tract, you can choose to sell either one independently, or both together, depending on what makes sense for your situation. Selling minerals while keeping the surface is common among Wyoming landowners who want to monetize the mineral asset without giving up the ranch or homestead itself.

sections.title: Figuring Out What You Own
sections.html:
The county clerk and recorder's deed records show whether your specific tract's surface and mineral estates are unified or split, and if split, when and how the separation happened. That record is where we start before ever discussing a number, because assuming you own both when the deed says otherwise is a mistake we want to catch before you do, not after.

Send us your legal description and county, and we'll pull the deed history to confirm exactly what mineral interest, if any, you hold, separate from whatever you may or may not own on the surface.

faqs.q: Can you own the surface of your land without owning the minerals?
faqs.a: Yes. This is common in Wyoming, where deeds frequently reserve or convey minerals separately from the surface. Many surface owners don't hold the mineral rights beneath their own land.

faqs.q: Does the mineral owner need your permission to drill on your surface property?
faqs.a: Generally not to drill, since the mineral estate is dominant under Wyoming law, but they typically owe you notice and, under the state's split estate statute, a surface use agreement or bond in many cases.

faqs.q: How do you find out if your land's surface and minerals are split?
faqs.a: The county clerk and recorder's deed records show the ownership history for your tract, including any historical reservation or severance of minerals from the surface.

faqs.q: Can you sell your minerals if you do not own the surface?
faqs.a: Yes. Mineral ownership and surface ownership transfer independently. Selling your minerals doesn't require involvement from or affect whoever owns the surface.

faqs.q: What is the Wyoming checkerboard and how does it relate to split estate?
faqs.a: It's the alternating pattern of private and federal land ownership across parts of southern Wyoming from 19th-century railroad grants, which affects both surface and mineral ownership patterns and whether development runs through a federal or private process.

image.alt: Surface vs. Mineral Estate mineral rights

items.name: Overriding Royalty Interests (ORRI)
items.meta: Hold an ORRI carved out of a Wyoming oil and gas lease? These interests expire with the lease. We buy ORRIs statewide.

sections.html:
An overriding royalty rides on top of a lease, not on top of the minerals themselves, which means it has a clock running that most owners don't realize until they try to sell.

An overriding royalty interest, or ORRI, is a share of production revenue carved out of a specific oil and gas lease, rather than out of the underlying mineral estate directly. It's typically created when a landman, geologist, or company assigns a lease to an operator but keeps a small royalty percentage for themselves as compensation, or when an operator sells down part of its position while retaining an override.

The critical thing that separates an ORRI from a mineral or landowner royalty interest is duration: an ORRI only exists as long as the lease it's carved from stays in force. If that lease expires, terminates, or gets released, the override goes with it, unlike a mineral or royalty interest tied to the land itself, which survives regardless of any particular lease's fate.

sections.title: Where ORRIs Usually Come From
sections.html:
In Wyoming's basins, ORRIs commonly trace back to landmen who assembled leasehold positions for an operator and kept an override as part of their compensation, or to smaller operators who farmed out drilling rights to a larger company while retaining a royalty slice. Some ORRIs have changed hands several times since creation, sold or inherited by people with no direct connection to the original oil and gas deal that produced them.

Because an ORRI isn't tied to land ownership the way a mineral interest is, you don't need to own any surface or minerals in Wyoming to hold one. We regularly buy ORRIs from owners who have no other connection to the state at all beyond this one carved-out interest.

sections.title: The Lease-Dependency Problem
sections.html:
Because your override lives inside a specific lease, its value depends heavily on that lease's remaining term, whether it's currently held by production, and how likely it is to stay in force. An ORRI attached to a lease that's been held by production from a strong, long-lived well is a fundamentally more durable asset than one attached to a lease nearing the end of its primary term with no production yet.

We check the underlying lease's status as part of every ORRI valuation — is it producing, is it held by production, is the primary term still running, has there been any assignment activity that might affect it. That lease-level detail matters more for an ORRI than for almost any other type of interest we buy.

sections.title: How ORRIs Get Valued
sections.html:
If the underlying lease has an active producing well, we value your override much like a royalty interest — based on current production, decline curve, and remaining reserves, adjusted for your specific override percentage. If the lease is undrilled or the well hasn't started producing, we look at the lease terms, remaining primary term, and area drilling activity, similar to how we'd approach a leased-but-undrilled mineral interest, but with the added lease-dependency factor built into the discount.

An override percentage is usually smaller than a landowner royalty, often a few percent rather than the eighth or higher common in landowner deals, and the value reflects that smaller share of production alongside the lease-dependency risk.

sections.title: Selling an Override
sections.html:
Overrides can be sold independently of the underlying mineral or working interest, and the buyer simply steps into your position for as long as the lease remains in force. Send us the assignment or conveyance document that created your ORRI, along with whatever you know about the lease and well it's tied to, and we'll research the current lease status before making an offer.

If you're not sure whether your override is still attached to an active lease, that's common, especially for ORRIs inherited or purchased secondhand, and it's exactly the kind of thing we check for you as part of the process.

faqs.q: What happens to your ORRI if the lease it's tied to expires?
faqs.a: The override typically ends when the lease terminates, since it's carved out of that specific lease rather than the underlying minerals. This is the key risk that separates an ORRI from a landowner royalty.

faqs.q: Do you need to own land or minerals in Wyoming to hold an ORRI?
faqs.a: No. An ORRI is tied to a lease, not to land ownership, so you can hold one with no other connection to the property or the state.

faqs.q: How is an ORRI different from an NPRI?
faqs.a: An NPRI is carved from the underlying mineral estate and survives regardless of any particular lease. An ORRI is carved from a specific lease and ends if that lease ends.

faqs.q: Can you buy your ORRI if you do not know the current status of the underlying lease?
faqs.a: Yes. Send us the assignment document that created your override and we'll research the lease's current status as part of preparing an offer.

faqs.q: Is an ORRI generally worth less than a mineral royalty of the same percentage?
faqs.a: Often, because of the added risk that the underlying lease could expire, even though the percentage itself might look similar on paper.

image.alt: Overriding Royalty Interests (ORRI) mineral rights

items.name: Working Interests
items.meta: Own a working interest in a Wyoming well and tired of the cost calls? We buy operated and non-operated working interests statewide. Get an offer.

sections.html:
A working interest pays more than a royalty when a well does well, and costs you real money when it doesn't. If you're carrying that risk and want out, we buy working interests too.

A working interest is ownership in the right to explore for, develop, and produce oil and gas from a lease, along with the obligation to pay a proportionate share of drilling, completion, and ongoing operating costs. That's the fundamental difference from a royalty interest — a working interest owner shares in the upside of production, but also shares in the downside of a dry hole, an expensive workover, or a stretch of low prices that makes a marginal well cost more to run than it earns.

Most working interest owners in Wyoming fall into one of two categories: operators actively running the well themselves, or non-operated partners who put up capital alongside an operator and receive their share of production net of costs, without making day-to-day operating decisions. We buy both types, though the valuation approach differs.

sections.title: Operated vs. Non-Operated Working Interests
sections.html:
An operated working interest means you or your company runs the well — makes the operating decisions, manages the vendors, and carries the operational liability that goes with actually running oil and gas equipment. That's a real business, not a passive investment, and it's a different kind of asset than most of what we typically buy.

A non-operated working interest is more common among the individual owners we work with — you put capital into a well an operator runs, and you receive your proportionate share of revenue after your share of costs is deducted, without making operational decisions yourself. Division orders and joint interest billing statements track this net position, and that paperwork is central to how we value the interest.

sections.title: Why Cost Exposure Changes the Math
sections.html:
Unlike a royalty interest, a working interest's value depends heavily on the cost side, not only the production side. A well with strong gross production but high lease operating expenses, or one facing an upcoming expensive workover, might net far less than the gross numbers suggest, or even run negative in a low-price month. We look at your joint interest billing history specifically for this reason, since it shows the real net cash flow you've actually been receiving, not the theoretical gross alone.

Aging wells often see rising per-barrel operating costs as equipment needs more maintenance and production volumes shrink, which is a normal pattern but one that specifically erodes working interest value faster than it erodes royalty value, since the royalty owner never bears those costs in the first place.

sections.title: Federal Leases and Working Interest Obligations
sections.html:
Working interests tied to federal leases in Wyoming's checkerboard and BLM-administered acreage carry additional obligations beyond a private lease — bonding requirements, compliance with federal drilling and spacing rules, and BLM oversight of operations that a purely private working interest doesn't face. If your working interest sits on federal acreage, that adds a layer of regulatory exposure worth factoring into the decision to hold or sell.

We check whether a working interest is tied to a federal or private lease as part of every valuation, since it affects both the ongoing obligations you're carrying and how a transfer of the interest needs to be documented and approved.

sections.title: Selling Out of a Working Interest
sections.html:
A lot of non-operated working interest owners came into their position through a family investment, a direct participation deal from years back, or an inherited share of a small operator's project, and many would rather have a clean exit than keep receiving joint interest billing statements and covering occasional cost calls indefinitely. Selling converts that ongoing cost and revenue exposure into a single payment and ends your liability going forward.

Send us your joint interest billing history, division order, and any operating agreement you have, and we'll review the net cash flow, remaining reserves, and cost trend before making a written offer that reflects the real economics of your specific interest.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a working interest and a royalty interest?
faqs.a: A working interest shares in both production revenue and the costs of drilling and operating the well. A royalty interest receives revenue only, with no cost exposure.

faqs.q: Do you have to be actively involved in operating the well to own a working interest?
faqs.a: No. Many working interest owners hold a non-operated position, contributing capital and sharing in net revenue while an operator handles the actual drilling and operating decisions.

faqs.q: Why would your working interest lose money in a given month?
faqs.a: If operating costs, including maintenance, workovers, or low commodity prices, exceed your share of gross production revenue that month, a working interest can net negative, unlike a royalty interest that never bears those costs.

faqs.q: Does selling a working interest end your obligation to pay future costs?
faqs.a: Yes. Once sold and properly assigned, the buyer takes on the ongoing cost and revenue position, and your obligation for future joint interest billing ends.

faqs.q: Is a working interest on a federal lease different from one on a private lease?
faqs.a: Yes. Federal leases carry additional bonding and compliance requirements through the BLM. We factor that into both valuation and the transfer process.

basins.title: Wyoming Basins

items.name: Powder River Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: Own minerals in Campbell or Converse County? Coalbed and shale ground carry separate records across the basin.

sections.html:
The Powder River Basin sits under Campbell and Converse counties, and it's carried three different plays in forty years. Whatever formation your deed touches, we can put a number on it.

Gillette is the county seat for Campbell County and the working center of the basin. Douglas anchors Converse County to the south. Between them the basin has produced coalbed methane out of the Fort Union and Wyodak coals, vertical oil out of the Muddy and Sussex, and now horizontal wells targeting the Niobrara and Turner shale in stacked laterals that run a mile or two under several sections at once.

That stacking is why an old deed can be worth revisiting. A tract that only ever produced a shallow coalbed methane well in the 1990s may now sit under a Niobrara unit two thousand feet deeper, with different operators, different royalty terms, and a different check size than what the family has seen for twenty years.

sections.title: Coalbed Methane vs. the Deeper Shale
sections.html:
Coalbed methane wells in the basin came in fast in the late 1990s and early 2000s, produced hard for a few years, and declined steep after that. A lot of Campbell County royalty owners are still getting checks off those wells, but the checks have thinned to a trickle compared to the first few years. If that's your only production, the value in your mineral rights is mostly future, not present cash flow.

The Niobrara and Turner shale wells drilled since roughly 2010 are a different animal — longer laterals, bigger frac jobs, and royalty streams that can run strong for a decade before the steep part of the decline curve hits. If a horizontal well has been permitted or drilled on your section in the last few years, that changes what your minerals are worth even if the well isn't producing yet.

sections.title: Who's Drilling Where
sections.html:
Chesapeake, EOG, and Devon have all held acreage and operated wells in the Powder River over the last decade, with names on the division order changing as properties trade hands. Continental Resources and Peak Resources have also been active in the Turner and Niobrara horizontal program. None of that operator history guarantees your specific section gets drilled next, but it tells you the basin is still being worked, not abandoned.

Spacing units in the horizontal program typically run a full section or larger, so one lateral well can hold interests across several separate tracts. If your mineral acres sit inside a unit with an active or recently completed well, your interest is easier to value with a real number instead of a guess, because there's a division order and check history to point to.

sections.title: The Checkerboard Runs Through Here Too
sections.html:
Southern Campbell County and northern Converse County both carry pieces of the old Union Pacific railroad grant checkerboard, alternating sections of private and federal mineral ownership left over from the 1862 Pacific Railway Act land grants. If your section is one of the odd-numbered railroad sections, your mineral ownership is likely private and clean of federal lease terms. If it's an even section, the federal government may hold some or all of the minerals, and any well draining that section has to account for a federal lease alongside private ones.

That split matters for a buyer because federal minerals carry different royalty rates, different assignment paperwork through the BLM, and slower closing timelines than a straight private deed. We check county records and, where it applies, BLM lease status before we ever put a number in front of you, so the offer already accounts for whether your acres are checkerboard-complicated or clean private minerals.

sections.title: What Your County Records Actually Show
sections.html:
Campbell and Converse County clerk and recorder offices hold every deed, lease, and division order affecting your tract, and that paper trail is where we start before we ever call you with a number. A deed that reserved minerals in the 1970s, a lease that's been held by production since the coalbed days, an assignment that changed operators three times — all of it shows up in the courthouse record, and all of it changes what your interest is actually worth today.

We pull that record ourselves rather than asking you to dig through a filing cabinet. If your fractional interest is small, or the chain of title has a gap, or there's an old lease still technically in force, we sort through it and explain what it means before you sign anything.

faqs.q: Your minerals only ever produced from a coalbed methane well. Are they still worth anything?
faqs.a: Often yes, but the value depends on whether the coalbed well is still paying and whether a deeper horizontal well could reach the same section. We look at both the current royalty stream and the deeper potential before we offer a number.

faqs.q: How do you find out if your section is checkerboard federal or private?
faqs.a: The county clerk and recorder's plat records and, for federal tracts, BLM lease records show it. We pull that history as part of every offer so you don't have to track it down yourself.

faqs.q: Does it matter which operator is on your division order?
faqs.a: It matters for how reliable and how fast the royalty payments run, and it factors into how we price the interest. A well operated by a company with a long track record in the basin values differently than a marginal or stripper operation.

faqs.q: You have Converse County minerals with no production history at all. Can you still buy them?
faqs.a: Yes. Undeveloped acreage in an active basin still has value tied to nearby drilling activity, spacing trends, and lease bonus history in the area, even with no royalty check yet.

faqs.q: Do you buy small fractional interests, like an eighth or a sixteenth?
faqs.a: Yes, fractional interests are common in this basin from decades of inheritance splits, and we buy them regularly. The offer reflects the fraction and the underlying acreage, not a flat minimum.

items.name: Green River Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: Minerals under Sublette or Sweetwater County? The Jonah and Pinedale tight-gas fields have paid royalties for two decades.

sections.html:
Sublette and Sweetwater counties sit on top of two of the tightest gas plays ever drilled in this country. If your family holds minerals under Jonah or the Pinedale Anticline, the field record is already well documented.

Pinedale is the county seat of Sublette County and gives its name to the Pinedale Anticline, one of the densest gas fields in the Rockies. Rock Springs, the seat of Sweetwater County, sits closer to the southern end of the basin near the Jonah Field. Both fields produce from the Lance and Mesaverde formations, tight sandstone that took modern completion technology to produce economically, which is why a lot of this acreage didn't see real drilling until the 2000s even though the gas had been known about for decades.

Because the pay zones are stacked and the wells are drilled in tight, dense patterns, a single 40 or 80-acre spacing unit here can carry a lot more wellbores than you'd see in a conventional field. That density is good for a mineral owner because more wells means more chances your specific tract is directly under production instead of just near it.

sections.title: Jonah and Pinedale Aren't the Same Field
sections.html:
Jonah Field sits mostly in Sublette County near the Sweetwater County line and was developed earlier and more densely than Pinedale, with wells spaced as tight as ten acres in the core. Pinedale Anticline covers a larger footprint north of Jonah and has produced for longer, with development continuing on federal leases well into the last several years. Knowing which field, or which edge of which field, your minerals sit in changes the offer, because the two areas have different well counts per section and different remaining reserve estimates.

Operators here have included Ultra Petroleum in the earlier development years, with Jonah Energy, PDC Energy, and Marathon holding significant positions more recently as the fields have traded hands. A change in operator doesn't change your ownership, but it can change how fast division orders get processed and how the royalty statement looks.

sections.title: Federal Minerals Dominate This Basin
sections.html:
Unlike southern Wyoming's railroad checkerboard, most of the federal minerals in Sublette and Sweetwater counties sit in large contiguous blocks rather than an alternating pattern, because this ground was never part of the Union Pacific land grant corridor. That's actually simpler for a buyer to evaluate in one sense — you're either sitting on private fee minerals or you're not — but it also means a much larger share of the basin's total production runs through BLM-administered leases with federal royalty terms rather than private lease terms.

If your deed traces back to a private mineral reservation that predates the federal leasing here, or you're one of the smaller number of owners holding fee minerals inside these fields, that's a meaningfully different asset than an interest tied to a federal allotment, and we price it accordingly after checking the reservation language.

sections.title: Tight Gas Decline Behaves Differently Than Shale Oil
sections.html:
Tight gas wells in the Lance and Mesaverde tend to decline steeply in year one, then flatten into a long, shallow tail that can keep paying for fifteen or twenty years at a modest rate. If your royalty checks have dropped sharply from an early peak but have been fairly steady for a few years since, that's the tail behavior, not a sign the well is dying. It changes how we model the remaining value of your interest compared to a fresh horizontal oil well still on its early decline.

Natural gas price swings hit this basin harder than an oil-weighted play, since almost everything produced here is gas with associated liquids. Your royalty check size has probably moved with Henry Hub pricing more than with anything happening at the wellhead, and that's a normal, expected pattern for Green River Basin production, not a red flag.

sections.title: What We Check Before Making an Offer
sections.html:
Sublette and Sweetwater County records show the deed history, any producing leases, and whether your tract sits inside a currently drilled spacing unit or an undeveloped fringe. We also check BLM lease status where the minerals are federal, since that record shows royalty rate, lease term, and whether the lease is currently held by production.

Send us your legal description or a copy of your deed and a recent division order or royalty statement if you have one, and we'll come back with a written offer that reflects which field, which formation, and which ownership type your minerals actually are.

faqs.q: Is Jonah Field better than Pinedale for mineral value?
faqs.a: Neither is universally better. Jonah was developed earlier and denser in its core, while Pinedale has a larger footprint with ongoing federal-lease development. We evaluate your specific section rather than the field name alone.

faqs.q: Why did your royalty check drop so much after the first year or two?
faqs.a: Tight gas wells in this basin decline fast early, then settle into a long, shallow tail. A drop from an early peak followed by steadier payments since is normal decline behavior, not necessarily a failing well.

faqs.q: Are most Green River Basin minerals federal or private?
faqs.a: A large share of production here runs through federal BLM leases in big contiguous blocks, different from the alternating railroad checkerboard further south. Some tracts are still private fee minerals, and we check the deed history to confirm which you hold.

faqs.q: Does a change in operator affect your ownership?
faqs.a: No. Ultra Petroleum, Jonah Energy, PDC Energy, and Marathon have all held positions here over time as properties traded. Your ownership stays the same; only the name issuing your division order changes.

faqs.q: Your minerals aren't producing yet. Can you still make an offer?
faqs.a: Yes. Undeveloped tracts near active spacing units in Sublette or Sweetwater County still carry value tied to development trends and lease bonus activity nearby, even before a well is drilled.

items.name: Niobrara Mineral Rights
items.meta: The DJ Basin's Niobrara play crosses into Laramie and Goshen counties. Owners near Cheyenne and Torrington start with the Laramie or Goshen County record.

sections.html:
Most people talk about the Niobrara as a Colorado play, but it crosses the state line into Laramie and Goshen counties, and the mineral ownership up here is priced differently than it is south of the border.

Cheyenne is the county seat of Laramie County, and Torrington is the county seat of Goshen County to the northeast. The DJ Basin's Niobrara chalk runs south from here into Colorado, but the northern edge of the play — the Silo Field near Cheyenne and acreage around Hawk Springs and Chugwater — has its own drilling history going back to the 1980s, well before the horizontal boom made the Niobrara a household name further south.

Because this is the flank of the play rather than the core, well results here vary more section to section than they do in the thickest part of the chalk down in Weld County, Colorado. That makes local production history, not only the play name on a map, the thing that actually sets what your minerals are worth.

sections.title: Silo Field and the Older Vertical Wells
sections.html:
Silo Field, straddling the Wyoming-Colorado line in Laramie County, was one of the first places anyone drilled the Niobrara chalk specifically, with vertical wells going in during the late 1980s and early 1990s. A lot of those original wells are long since stripper production or plugged, but the field proved the chalk would produce here, and it's part of why operators came back decades later with horizontal technology aimed at the same rock.

If your family's minerals trace back to a lease from that earlier vertical era, the original lease terms and even the original well may still be relevant to your title, even though the economics of the play have completely changed since then. We look at both the old lease history and current activity nearby before pricing an interest like this.

sections.title: The Railroad Checkerboard Reaches Cheyenne
sections.html:
Laramie County sits right on the original Union Pacific transcontinental line, which means the checkerboard pattern of alternating private railroad sections and federal sections runs directly through some of this acreage. It's the same 1862 Pacific Railway Act grant that checkerboards the Powder River Basin further north, just at the other end of the line. A section a few miles from Cheyenne can be entirely private minerals while the section next to it is federal, with no visible difference on the ground.

That matters here specifically because a horizontal Niobrara well can be permitted to drain both a private and a federal section in the same unit, which means your royalty deck might include both privately negotiated and federally set terms depending on exactly which section your minerals sit in. We verify that against county plat records before quoting a number.

sections.title: Flank Position Changes the Math
sections.html:
The core of the Niobrara chalk thickens and gets more consistently productive as you move south into Colorado. Up here on the Wyoming side, the chalk is thinner in places and well results have more spread between a strong producer and a mediocre one. That doesn't mean your minerals are worth less on principle, but it does mean we weight nearby actual well performance more heavily than basin-wide averages when we evaluate a Laramie or Goshen County tract.

Goshen County, further from the historic Silo development, has seen less drilling overall, so acreage there is priced more on lease bonus and permitting trends than on an established royalty stream for most owners. If you're in Goshen County with undeveloped minerals, that's a normal position for this part of the play, not a sign your acreage is worthless.

sections.title: Getting to a Number
sections.html:
We start with the Laramie or Goshen County clerk's deed and lease records to confirm what you actually own and whether it's inside the checkerboard's private or federal pattern. From there we look at any producing wells on or near your section, whether from the original Silo-era verticals or newer horizontal work, and current permitting activity in the area.

Send us your legal description, county, and any lease or division order paperwork you have, and we'll get back to you with a written offer, explained in plain terms, that reflects where exactly your minerals sit in this play.

faqs.q: Is the Wyoming Niobrara the same as the Colorado Niobrara?
faqs.a: Same formation, different position in the play. The Colorado side around Weld County is the thick core; the Wyoming side around Laramie and Goshen counties is the northern flank, with thinner chalk and more variable well results.

faqs.q: What is Silo Field?
faqs.a: Silo Field is an older Niobrara chalk field straddling the Laramie County, Wyoming and Weld County, Colorado line, first drilled with vertical wells in the late 1980s. It's one of the earliest proven Niobrara producing areas.

faqs.q: How do you know if your Laramie County section is checkerboard federal or private?
faqs.a: County plat and deed records show the original Union Pacific grant pattern. We check this as part of every offer, since it directly affects royalty terms and closing paperwork.

faqs.q: Your Goshen County minerals have never produced. Are they worth anything?
faqs.a: Undeveloped Goshen County acreage is priced mainly on nearby lease bonus and permitting trends rather than an existing royalty stream, which is typical for this part of the basin. We can still make an offer on it.

faqs.q: Why does flank position matter for value?
faqs.a: Well results near the edge of any chalk play vary more than they do in the thick core, so we weight actual nearby well performance more heavily than basin averages when pricing a flank-position tract.
